extracted_data.study_region_context: China (domain: 14.75°N–55.75°N, 69.75°E–139.75°E). Results reported for whole-country and subregions (Yangtze River basin, Southeastern China, Central/Northern/Northeast China). Seasonal stratification into winter, spring (Win-Spr) and summer, autumn (Sum-Aut); no Köppen classes or elevation bands explicitly used.
extracted_data.target_variable: Two-week total precipitation (forecast target: sum of ensuing 14 days). NOTE: This study does NOT perform dew-point (Tdew) reconstruction; relative humidity (sigma level 0.995) and 2 m temperature are used as predictors but dew point is not reconstructed.
extracted_data.predictors_used: 21 candidate predictors including: 2 m temperature, relative humidity at sigma level 0.995, surface pressure, geopotential height PCs at 10 hPa, sea ice concentration, Pacific SST PCs, CFSv2 total precipitation (forecast), MJO phase/amplitude, MEI, indices AO, WNPM, WNPSH1, WNPSH2, plus lagged ('shift x') and anomalous ('anom') variants of some predictors and an intercept ('ones'). Predictors were interpolated to 1°×1° grid. (Only Tmin-specific dew-point predictors like Tmin→Tdew formulae are NOT used here.)
extracted_data.baseline_assumptions_compared: Compared against dynamical model CFSv2 operational forecasts (skill ~0.11). Also compared MultiLLR variants: 21-index baseline, 21-index+AO, 21-index+WNPM, 21-index+WNPSH; ensemble (equal-weight) of 21-index+AO MultiLLR with CFSv2 (skill improvement to 0.16). Climatology is used to compute anomalies for predictors/skill (daily climatology 1980–2010 or 1981–2010) but no FAO-56 Tdew≈Tmin or explicit dew-point climatology baseline is evaluated.
extracted_data.method_model_type: Local linear regression fit independently at each grid point (LLR) combined with multitask backward stepwise feature selection (MultiLLR). Also tested AutoKNN analog method (local linear regression with 20 nearest historical analog dates). Details: candidate regressors include intercept, anomalies, lagged ('shift x') versions; feature selection based on forecast performance using spatial cosine similarity.
extracted_data.seasonal_dayofyear_pooling: Seasonality handled via anomalies relative to daily climatology (anom suffix) computed over 1980–2010 (predictor anomalies) and removal of climatological annual cycle over 1981–2010 for skill calculation. Predictors (except MJO) averaged over ensuing 2 weeks to match the 14-day precipitation target. No explicit moving-window LOESS/DOY kernel bandwidths reported.
extracted_data.localization_stratification: Localization achieved by fitting regression coefficients separately at each grid point (per-grid LLR). Multitask feature selection pools information spatially using spatial cosine similarity to evaluate candidate predictors, but no explicit climate-zone or elevation-band stratification was reported.
extracted_data.anomaly_definition: Predictor anomalies (suffix 'anom') are defined as departures from daily climatology computed over 1980–2010 (paper text). For forecast-skill computation anomalies were obtained by removing the climatological annual cycle during 1981–2010 (paper uses this baseline for Y and Ŷ when computing spatial cosine similarity).
extracted_data.autoregressive_or_lag_terms: The candidate regressors include lagged versions indicated by 'shift x' (hysteresis characteristic from previous x days based on data update timing), i.e., predictors with explicit lags; however the paper does not report explicit autoregressive terms on the predictand (precipitation) such as P(t-1) or modeled AR(p) on residuals. AutoKNN experiment uses historical-date analogs (20 dates) rather than AR coefficients.
extracted_data.accuracy_metrics: Forecast skill measured by spatial cosine similarity between observed and predicted anomalies. Reported values: average skill across 2011–2016 = 0.11 (21-index model); 21-index+AO = 0.13; CFSv2 = 0.11; ensemble (21-index+AO + CFSv2 equal weight) = 0.16. Seasonal: winter skill > 0.21, summer skill ≈ 0.0, autumn and spring intermediate. AutoKNN gave negative skill. No RMSE/MAE/Bias or dew-point-specific metrics are reported in this paper.
extracted_data.validation_design: Forecasted 26 target dates per year (every 2 weeks) for 2011–2016 → 156 forecasts. For each forecast date the training range spans from the first year when all selected predictor data are available up to the year of the target date. Evaluation across high-skill vs low-skill years and by seasons (Win-Spr vs Sum-Aut). Predictors and reanalysis interpolated to 1°×1°. No station-level holdout or cross-validated dew-point reconstruction experiments (study focused on gridded precipitation forecasting).
extracted_data.reported_skill_mechanisms: Authors attribute skill to teleconnection/large-scale drivers and land/ocean influences: MJO and surface pressure (cold surge) identified as important predictors; AO and WNPSH also improve skill (AO most helpful). Physical mechanisms invoked include modulation of southern-branch trough (SBT) and middle-east jet stream (MEJS), northward moisture transport/convergence, and intraseasonal modulation of convection (MJO). Soil moisture, SST, sea ice, and land surface processes are cited in intro as potential sources of subseasonal predictability though not all were primary predictors here.
extracted_data.interpretation_of_broad_smoothing: Predictors (except MJO) are averaged over the ensuing 2-week target period to be consistent with the 14-day precipitation sum—this broad temporal pooling is used to match target temporal scale and reduce noise. The paper also uses daily climatology anomalies (1980–2010) implying a smoothed seasonal cycle baseline; no detailed theoretical justification for broader DOY/window widths beyond matching target averaging and sample-size considerations is given.
extracted_data.physical_constraints_or_qc: No explicit physical-constraint post-processing (e.g., clipping dew point to ≤ air temperature) is reported because the target is precipitation. Data handling steps include interpolation of reanalysis predictors to 1°×1° and consistency checks on predictor availability for training range. No special QC for humidity/psychrometric conversions or sensor wetting is described.
extracted_data.failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint: The paper does NOT report any failure modes related to dew-point or unrealistically high dew-point estimates (no dew-point reconstruction performed). Reported failure modes for the precipitation task: markedly low skill in summer and autumn, poor seasonal-mean prediction in Southeastern China, tendency for model to predict drought-like anomalies (negative seasonal-mean bias), and AutoKNN delivering negative skill.
extracted_data.hypothesized_failure_mechanisms: For poor performance the authors mention (a) physical reasons: seasonality and local weather complexity (summer/autumn precipitation patterns are harder to predict), influence of teleconnection factors varying by season (WNPM was found to be a negative contributor), and possibly insufficient representation of moisture transport processes; and (b) methodological/data reasons: limitation of using only local linear regression (authors note model simplicity limits skill), insufficient/irrelevant predictors for some regions/seasons, and potential sampling/training-range limitations. No sensor wetting, Tmin biases, or reanalysis humidity artifact hypotheses are discussed in the context of dew-point extremes.
extracted_data.climate_zone_specific_findings: Performance breakdown by region/season: better representation of intraseasonal variability (ISV) and higher skill in Yangtze River and Southeastern China during Win-Spr in high-skill years; expansion of strong ISV to Central/Northern/Northeast China in Sum-Aut but model underestimates ISV there; Southeastern China seasonal-mean precipitation particularly poorly captured. No explicit comparisons by arid vs humid or high-elevation vs lowland zones; no tropical lowland dew-point-specific analyses.
extracted_data.key_equations_or_parameterizations: The paper provides the forecast-skill metric: forecast_skill(Y, Ŷ) = <Y, Ŷ> / (||Y||2 * ||Ŷ||2) where Y are observed anomalies and Ŷ predicted anomalies. No equations or parameterizations relating Tmin to dew point (e.g., FAO-56 Tdew≈Tmin or vapor-pressure regression) appear in this paper.
extracted_data.data_sources: Observations: CN05.1 daily precipitation dataset from China National Climate Center (1961–2017). Predictors: NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis (daily 2 m temperature, relative humidity at sigma level 0.995, surface pressure, geopotential height), NOAA/ESRL MJO, MEI from Australian Bureau of Meteorology, OISST (NOAA) SST and sea-ice concentration, CFSv2 operational 6-hourly forecast precipitation (averaged to 14-day), AO from CPC; WNPM and WNPSH indices derived from reanalysis fields. Predictors interpolated to 1°×1° grid and averaged over ensuing 2 weeks.
extracted_data.notable_limitations_caveats: Authors note the MultiLLR used only local linear regression which likely limits forecast skill and suggest testing more suitable methods. Seasonal nonstationarity, limited ability to predict summer/autumn precipitation, and regional failures (Southeastern China) are highlighted. The study did not attempt dew-point reconstruction, so no dew-point-specific validation or QC is available. Training ranges vary by target date depending on predictor availability.

extracted_data.name_full: Kriging-based dew point interpolation with altitude lapse-rate correction and Fourier-seasonal anomaly kriging (Chabot-Couture et al. 2014)
extracted_data.brief_description: A method to build daily gridded dew point and relative-humidity maps by (1) removing seasonal harmonics (0–3× yearly) from station time series to form anomalies, (2) fitting day-of-year semi-variograms (sill and half-correlation distance) across 30 years, (3) kriging zero-altitude-equivalent dew point, and (4) reintroducing altitude using a day-of-year lapse rate; RH is computed from gridded T and Tdew using the August–Roche–Magnus formula.
extracted_data.study_region_context: Primary test region: Madagascar (tropical island; mix of humid lowlands, eastern moist forests, drier western interior, and mountainous interior); broader context: Africa (stations across Africa used for method and error mapping). Periods: station data 1981–2010 (Madagascar cross-validation), RFE rainfall 2001–2010; referenced WorldClim climate normals (1950–2000 baseline). Elevation considered explicitly via lapse rates; method notes differences between lowlands and high elevations and seasonal dry vs wet seasons.
extracted_data.target_variable: Dew-point temperature (T_d, °C) and Relative Humidity (RH, %). RH computed from T and T_d via August–Roche–Magnus approximation.
extracted_data.predictors_used: Primary predictors: observed station dew point and air temperature time series (GSOD network). Supporting predictors/covariates: elevation (altitude) via derived dew-point lapse rate (day-of-year dependent), WorldClim daily climate-normal temperature surface (adds systematic/mean field), Fourier-seasonal components (0,1,2,3×year) removed to form anomalies, spatial distance kernels (semi-variogram) for kriging; for land-surface-temperature completion they used temporal autocorrelation (pixel-wise) and regional daily-average anomaly as additional weight. The method does not use Tmin alone as predictor; it uses station T_d measurements when available.
extracted_data.baseline_assumptions_compared: Compared interpolation results against the supporting climate layer (WorldClim) as the mean offset; authors note that WorldClim climate-layer error (~<1°C) produces a systematic bias in air temperature estimates. The paper also cites literature recommending Tmin as an acceptable proxy when Tdew is unavailable (Kimball et al. 1997) but does not adopt Tmin-only baselines itself. No explicit comparison to FAO-56 Tdew≈Tmin is reported in this paper.
extracted_data.method_model_type: Spatial statistical interpolation: simple kriging of day-to-day anomalies (anomalies derived by subtracting orthogonalized Fourier harmonics 0–3× yearly). Variogram functional form used: γ(d) = γ(∞) (1 - 1/(1-(d/λ)^2)) with day-of-year-specific fits. Dew point: station measurements corrected to zero-altitude using a region-specific, day-of-year lapse rate (derived from 30 years of (altitude, dew point) pairs), kriged at zero-altitude, then altitude effect added back. Temporal completion for MODIS LST used temporal kriging with a fitted autocorrelation (power-law) and a linear combination with regional daily anomaly weighted by remaining variance. Smoothing of variogram parameters via median and mean 31‑day sliding windows. No explicit machine‑learning models used; algorithmic, geostatistical approach.
extracted_data.seasonal_dayofyear_pooling: Seasonality removed by Fourier subtraction of constant plus 1×, 2×, 3× yearly harmonics (orthogonalized over valid measurements). Semi-variogram parameters (sill and half-correlation distance) fit independently for each day-of-year across 30 years of station pairs, then smoothed by two passes: median in a 31-day sliding window followed by a 31-day moving average; dew-point lapse rate day-of-year curve smoothed similarly (31-day median then 31-day average). Land-surface STD calculated with a 31-day weighted window (weights w(t)=1-|t/16|^3).
extracted_data.localization_stratification: Localization via (a) region selection for lapse-rate derivation (region should contain sufficient stations without encompassing very different climates), (b) day-of-year specific variogram fitting across stations within the region, and (c) altitude adjustment using a region-wide, day-of-year dew-point lapse rate. Spatial heterogeneity handled by kriging weights derived from fitted semi-variograms; no explicit climate-zone classification (e.g., Koppen) used, though authors discuss differing station densities and climate behaviour across Africa and Madagascar.
extracted_data.anomaly_definition: Anomalies = station time-series minus seasonal signal where seasonality = orthogonalized Fourier harmonics (0th, 1st, 2nd, 3rd annual harmonics) computed over valid observations. For land-surface temperature anomalies they also standardized by seasonally-varying STD to obtain zero mean, unit std 'normalized-departure' time series.
extracted_data.autoregressive_or_lag_terms: Explicit autoregressive/lag modeling used for MODIS land surface temperature temporal completion: pixel-wise autocorrelation functions fitted (power-law), and only valid measurements within the maximum useful lag (lag until autocorr becomes negative) were included in temporal kriging. No explicit AR terms (T_d(t-1), etc.) are reported for station dew point or air temperature kriging; interpolation is spatial kriging of daily anomalies rather than time-series AR modeling.
extracted_data.accuracy_metrics: Dew point (Madagascar cross-validation, medians across 26 stations): daily median bias = -0.177°C; median MAE = 1.25°C; median RMSE = 1.64°C; median 95th-percentile absolute error = 3.32°C. 10-day median bias = -0.289°C; 10-day 95th percentile abs error = 2.27°C. Relative humidity (derived from interpolated T and T_d): daily median bias = +3.09 percentage points; median MAE = 6.61%; median RMSE = 8.38%; median 95th-percentile absolute error = 16.6%; 10-day 95th-percentile = 11.0%. Air temperature interpolation: median daily bias = -0.786°C; median MAE = 1.21°C; median RMSE = 1.47°C; median 95th-percentile abs error = 2.75°C.
extracted_data.validation_design: Cross-validation via leave‑one‑station-out comparisons across weather stations in Madagascar: errors summarized as medians across 26 weather stations (Madagascar). For Africa-wide station reporting counts they report numbers: of 1403 GSOD stations, 923 met quality criteria for air temperature (1981–2011), 914 for dew point. Validation compares kriging-predicted distributions to observed station values and to Kriging-predicted error estimates.
extracted_data.reported_skill_mechanisms: Authors attribute skill to: (a) removal of systematic seasonal cycle via Fourier decomposition so kriging operates on anomalies with zero mean, (b) use of a high-resolution climate normal (WorldClim) to represent systematic geography/altitude effects and reduce spatial extrapolation error, (c) day-of-year-specific variogram fits capture seasonal changes in spatial correlation length/variability, and (d) altitude correction via observed dew-point lapse rate accounts for orographic effects and moisture decrease with altitude. The method outperforms naïve climatology in areas with station coverage because kriging captures day-to-day weather anomalies; errors are dominated by climate-layer bias far from stations.
extracted_data.interpretation_of_broad_smoothing: The paper argues for smoothing variogram/lapse-rate parameters over a 31‑day window (median then mean) to stabilize day-of-year fits given noisy/irregular station reporting; this broad (31-day) pooling reduces variance in parameter estimates while retaining seasonal structure. They imply wide windows help when station samples are limited and when seasonal signals vary smoothly across DOY.
extracted_data.physical_constraints_or_qc: Quality-control and physical constraints applied: station inclusion criteria (≥61 valid measurements within any 365-day window; no more than 30 consecutive days of zero reporting in DOY histogram; longest missing window ≤30 days), outlier removal for land-surface time series (values >4σ removed and iteratively recomputed), replacement/clip rules for rainfall (RFE 2.0 values >300 mm/day set to 300 mm/day; missing → 0), treatment of pathological MODIS pixels (require ≥61 valid measurements/year or completion from neighbors), optional capping of RH at 100% recommended when interpolated T_d > T_air. Nugget effect considered in variogram when neighboring stations report incongruent values to avoid numerical instability.
extracted_data.failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint: Reported failure modes: (1) interpolated dew point sometimes exceeds interpolated air temperature producing RH>100%; authors suggest user may cap RH at 100% or interpret as indication of precipitation; (2) Kriging numerical instability/overshoot when semi-variogram lacks nugget or neighboring stations disagree; (3) remote-sensing LST completion fails in very cloudy regions (e.g., southern India monsoon) where large contiguous 'pathological pixels' prevent Fourier extraction; (4) systematic bias due to WorldClim climate-layer error (~<1°C) producing negative bias in predicted T and consequent RH bias.
extracted_data.hypothesized_failure_mechanisms: Physical meteorology reasons discussed: (a) orographic precipitation and relief affect dew-point lapse rates and local moisture (environmental dew-point lapse rate larger than air temperature lapse rate, except during dry season), (b) cloudiness affects satellite LST (daytime cooling and nighttime warming) and thus errors in LST-derived temperature fields, (c) regional seasonality (wet vs dry season) changes lapse rates and RH-altitude relationships. Data/model artifacts discussed: (a) sparse/stationary-biased networks and large station-free regions increase kriging error and produce interpolation artifacts, (b) absence of nugget in variogram or unconstrained kriging can overshoot measurements, (c) climate-normal layer bias (WorldClim) introduces systematic offsets, (d) MODIS missing data and aggregation biases (8/16/30-day composites bias clear-sky), (e) RFE satellite limitations (underestimate warm-cloud/orographic precipitation) and clipped rainfall values. Sensor wetting or ventilation issues are noted indirectly as possible short-range measurement errors but not detailed.
extracted_data.climate_zone_specific_findings: Authors report: (a) near-equatorial regions have lower 10-day air-temperature variability (~0.5°C) leading to smaller kriging error even when stations are sparse; (b) 10-day temperature variability increases with latitude to ~2.5°C at 30° latitude; (c) dew-point lapse rate is season-dependent in Madagascar and generally larger than air-temp lapse rate except during dry season; (d) relative humidity tends to decrease with altitude except in parts of the dry season; (e) MODIS LST day vs night behaviour differs by land-cover and altitude (daytime LST correlates with land-cover; nighttime LST correlates with altitude). No explicit Koppen-based stratified performance numbers are given, but contrasts between humid lowlands, montane regions, and dry-season behaviour are discussed qualitatively.
extracted_data.key_equations_or_parameterizations: Main equations: (1) Dew point → RH via August–Roche–Magnus: RH = exp( - a b (T - T_d) / ((b + T_d)(b + T)) ) with a=17.271, b=237.7°C. (2) Semi-variogram functional form used for kriging: γ(d) = γ(∞) (1 - 1/(1 - (d/λ)^2)), where γ(∞) is the sill and λ the half-correlation distance, fit per day-of-year. (3) LST reconstruction: LST_ij(t) = MEAN_ij(DOY) + STD_ij(DOY) × [G_ij(t) + E_ij(t) × A_avg(t)], where G is temporal-kriging guess, E remaining error term, and A_avg regional average anomaly. Seasonal decomposition: subtraction of 0-,1-,2-,3-yearly Fourier components (orthogonalized).
extracted_data.data_sources: Station data: GSOD (Global Summary of the Day) station air temperature and dew point; WorldClim monthly high-resolution climate normals (used for daily climate layer). Remote sensing: MODIS MYD11A1 v005 LST (Aqua); rainfall: RFE 2.0 (satellite merged estimator), comparisons with GPCC, CRU 2.1. Spatial resolution targeted: ~30 arc-seconds (~1 km) for final products; station records spanning 1981–2010 used for variogram fitting in Madagascar; RFE available from 2001 onward.
extracted_data.notable_limitations_caveats: Limitations noted: systematic bias from supporting WorldClim climate layer (~<1°C) affecting absolute temperature/dry-bias; kriging accuracy degrades far from stations and depends on spatial correlation lengths; MODIS LST completion fails in persistently cloudy regions (e.g., Indian monsoon); RFE 2.0 may underestimate warm-cloud/orographic precipitation and 10 years may be insufficient to average rainfall inhomogeneity; interpolation reduces extreme temporal/spatial rainfall variability compared with station-based products; relative humidity interpolation errors dominated by variability and climate-layer errors; authors caution that aggregated remote-sensing composites (8/16/30-day) bias clear-sky conditions and may misrepresent true daily variability.

extracted_data.name_full: VISEA daily near-surface air temperature estimation using the vegetation-index–land-surface-temperature (VI–Ts) triangle method
extracted_data.brief_description: Within the VISEA ET algorithm the authors estimate instantaneous daytime air temperature from the VI–Ts relationship (Nishida et al., 2003) using a local 5×5 grid scatter of VI vs. land surface temperature (Ts), assume the cold-edge Ts equals air temperature for fully vegetated pixels, extend day/night estimates with a sine–cosine diurnal curve, and take the 24 h mean as daily Ta used in subsequent radiation and ET calculations.
extracted_data.study_region_context: Global application; global 0.05° grid. Validation uses 149 FLUXNET towers (selected from 212) covering 12 IGBP land-cover types (CRO, CSH, DBF, DNF, EBF, ENF, GRA, MF, OSH, SAV, WET, WSA) across tropical humid lowlands, savannas, temperate/needleleaf forests, high-latitude cold regions and other climates. Flux-tower evaluation period mainly 2001–2015 (tower selection) and multi-product comparisons across 2001–2020.
extracted_data.target_variable: Daily near-surface air temperature (Ta, K) estimated as a 24 h average derived from satellite instantaneous estimates and sine–cosine diurnal extension; (the paper does not directly reconstruct dew point or vapor pressure).
extracted_data.predictors_used: MODIS land surface temperature (MOD11C1 Ts daytime and nighttime), MODIS vegetation index (MOD13C1 VI), neighboring 5×5 grid cell VI–Ts scatter, ERA5-Land hourly downward shortwave radiation (ERA5_Rd) used later for energy budget and daily net radiation, satellite albedo (MCD43C3) and emissivity (from MOD11C1), cloud-clearness index derived from ERA5_Rd, and (for nighttime) MOD11C1 nighttime Ts assumed equal to Ta. No use of simple Tmin-only regressions is reported for Ta estimation.
extracted_data.baseline_assumptions_compared: No explicit comparison to FAO-56 assumption Tdew ≈ Tmin or to dew-point-from-Tmin climatologies; VISEA compares radiation sources (ERA5 vs. CERES) and compares final ET against other ET products (GLEAM, FLUXCOM, MOD16, AVHRR, PML) and FLUXNET observations, but not against FAO-56 dew-point baseline.
extracted_data.method_model_type: Empirical physical hybrid: VI–Ts triangle method to infer instantaneous air temperature (local per-pixel using neighboring 5×5 grid scatter), interpolation along warm/cold edges to map VI->Ts_min (assumed Ta), then a sine–cosine diurnal fitting to produce hourly Ta profiles and a 24 h mean. This is embedded inside the VISEA Penman–Monteith-based ET framework which uses decoupling-parameter adjustments to convert instantaneous EF to daily EF. No machine-learning, AR, or kriging methods used for Ta estimation.
extracted_data.seasonal_dayofyear_pooling: Seasonality handled implicitly via (a) using current-day MODIS VI/Ts observations within a 5×5 spatial neighborhood to create the VI–Ts scatter (no explicit day-of-year pooling reported) and (b) using daily ERA5_Rd and daily cloud-clearness Kt. There is no reported explicit per-day-of-year regression, moving window (e.g., 7/30/45 d) for Ta estimation; gap-filling of missing MODIS days uses neighboring days (no explicit window width reported besides 'neighboring days'); FAO extraterrestrial radiation uses day-of-year (standard FAO formula) for Ra.
extracted_data.localization_stratification: Localization via spatial neighborhood (5×5 MODIS grid window) to build the VI–Ts triangle and identify warm/cold edges; flux-tower validation is stratified by IGBP land-cover types. No explicit climate-zone-specific regression models or elevation bands for Ta estimation are fitted within VISEA Ta method.
extracted_data.anomaly_definition: No use of anomalies (departures from climatology) or detrending described for Ta estimation; climatologies are used elsewhere (e.g., MODIS multi-year products) but not for anomaly-based Ta reconstruction.
extracted_data.autoregressive_or_lag_terms: None reported. No AR(p) or time-lagged dewpoint/humidity terms used for Ta or humidity reconstruction.
extracted_data.accuracy_metrics: Reported skill for VISEA_Ta against FLUXNET observations by land-cover: NSE ranged ~ -0.22 (worst, MF) to 0.82 (best, OSH); correlation R ranged ~0.44 to 0.97; RMSE ranged ~5.7 K (best) to 11.2 K (worst) depending on land-cover. For other variables relevant to humidity inference (ERA5_Rd): mean NSE 0.84, mean R 0.92, RMSE 38.3 W m^-2. ET (dependent product) has mean correlation around 0.6 and RMSE about 1.4 mm d^-1 (abstract); per-land-cover ET NSE values and RMSEs are reported in the paper and Table 3 and Figures 4–7.
extracted_data.validation_design: Validation vs. in situ FLUXNET2015 tower data: selected 149 towers fulfilling coverage (2001–2015 period), ERA5_Rd>0, and MODIS land-cover consistency; evaluation compares estimated Ta, net radiation, and ET against tower measurements. Multi-product comparison uses 5 independent gridded ET datasets (GLEAM, FLUXCOM, AVHRR, MOD16, PML) and GPCC precipitation. Validation metrics are computed monthly and daily and stratified by IGBP land-cover type; cross-validation or temporal holdout of training is not applicable because the VI–Ts method is an observational/local empirical procedure rather than a trained statistical model.
extracted_data.reported_skill_mechanisms: Authors explain why VI–Ts works: negative correlation between VI and Ts across mixed vegetation/bare patterns (warm edge from bare/dry pixels, cold edge from dense-vegetation pixels) allows estimation of minimum Ts (assumed Ta) via triangle geometry in VI–Ts space. The decoupling parameter (Ω) accounts for radiative vs aerodynamic control, converting instantaneous EF to daily EF, improving daily ET estimates. ERA5 radiation assimilation gives near-real-time energy forcing but errors in ERA5_Rd and mismatch between tower footprint and grid-average albedo/vegetation explain much of the bias. Soil moisture is recognised as a critical regulator for ET (buffering/recovery after rainfall) but is not included in Ta estimation.
extracted_data.interpretation_of_broad_smoothing: Authors implicitly prefer local spatial pooling (5×5) rather than broad seasonal pooling because the VI–Ts triangle relies on within-neighborhood contrasts in VI and Ts to identify warm/cold edges; they use neighboring days for gap-filling to reduce cloud-induced noise. No explicit statement that very broad day-of-year smoothing is superior; rather they point out that insufficient VI variance across a neighborhood (e.g., dense forest or homogeneous bare regions) undermines the method, implying a trade-off between sampling variance and locality.
extracted_data.physical_constraints_or_qc: Assumptions and QC noted: (1) for fully vegetated grid cells the minimum surface temperature is assumed equal to air temperature (Ta); (2) soil heat flux G ≈ 0 on daily basis; (3) excluded flux towers with zero ERA5_Rd and ensured tower site grid cells are land via MOD12C1; (4) emissivity from MOD11C1 used and atmospheric emissivity computed following Brutsaert (1975) and Wang & Dickinson (2013); (5) gap-filling of MODIS data uses neighboring days; (6) no explicit Tdew <= Ta clipping or RH bounds are discussed because dew point/humidity are not estimated directly in the paper.
extracted_data.failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint: The paper does not report explicit attempts to reconstruct dew point or humidity and thus does not report observed physically implausible dew points; however it reports failure modes of the Ta and ET estimation that would affect any downstream humidity/dew-point estimates: (a) VI–Ts method failure in dense forests, cold-season/temperate regions (positive VI–Ts correlation), and savannas during dry or wet seasons where VI variance is low, and (b) ERA5_Rd poor performance in savannas leading to large errors in net radiation and ET. The authors note systematic underestimation of net radiation (~30%) in some land covers which would bias any vapor-pressure-related reconstructions.
extracted_data.hypothesized_failure_mechanisms: Physical meteorology explanations given: (a) VI–Ts failure where vegetation growth correlates positively with Ts (temperate/cold regions) or where vegetation is homogeneous (deserts, dense forests) so warm/cold edges are not present; (b) savanna complexity (seasonal vegetation cover, cloudiness, aerosols, land-use change) complicates radiative transfer and ERA5 radiation simulation; (c) soil moisture buffering causes delayed ET response after rainfall (affects ET but would also affect humidity estimates if used); (d) scale mismatch between flux-tower footprint and 0.05° grid affects Rn comparisons. Data/QC/model artifacts: (a) ERA5_Rd biases (assimilation/model errors) especially over savannas; (b) gap-filling of MODIS (neighboring days) can introduce artifacts when cloud cover is persistent; (c) representativeness errors due to grid-mean albedo differing from tower footprint albedo; (d) the VI–Ts method's assumption that minimum Ts equals Ta may fail and propagate systematic bias into subsequent calculations.
extracted_data.climate_zone_specific_findings: Performance varies by land-cover/climate: best Ta performance in open shrubland (OSH), woody savanna (WSA), and grassland (GRA) (high NSE/R and low RMSE), poor performance in mixed forests (MF), savanna (SAV), and some croplands (CRO) where VI–Ts correlation breaks down. ERA5_Rd performs well overall but poorly in SAV (NSE=0.29, RMSE ~63.2 W m^-2). VISEA ET tends to underestimate ET in colder high-latitude regions and shows biases in savannas due to ERA5_Rd and Ta errors. Tropical humid lowlands have very high ET magnitudes (~1500 mm yr^-1) and VISEA can overestimate ET if water availability is not properly constrained.
extracted_data.key_equations_or_parameterizations: Key formulations used (paper equation references): (a) VI–Ts triangle to identify warm/cold edges and map VI to Ts (Nishida et al., 2003, described in paper sect. 2.1.3); (b) EF^i and EF^d relations: instantaneous EF^i (Eq. 4) and conversion to daily EF^d via decoupling parameter Ω and Δ (Eqs. 7–10); (c) daily available energy Q = R_n - G (Eq. 11) with R_n computed from downward shortwave, albedo, emissivities and downward longwave parametrized with cloud clearness (Eqs. 12–16); (d) daily ET^d = EF^d * Q^d (Eq. 17). The explicit Tmin->Tdew formula is not present because dew point is not estimated.
extracted_data.data_sources: MODIS products: MOD11C1 (LST/emissivity), MOD09CMG (surface reflectance), MCD43C3 (albedo), MOD13C1 (vegetation index), MCD12C1 (land cover) at 0.05°; ERA5-Land hourly downward shortwave radiation (ERA5_Rd) (0.1°, interpolated to 0.05° for use); FLUXNET2015 towers (149 selected) for validation; additional gridded ET products for comparison: GLEAM, FLUXCOM, AVHRR ET, MOD16, PML; precipitation from GPCC and CPC used in drought case analysis. Time periods: tower comparisons use 2001–2015 (tower selection), multi-product comparisons across ~2001–2020 (varies by product). CERES was used in a sensitivity test for incident radiation.
extracted_data.notable_limitations_caveats: Authors note key limitations: (1) VI–Ts fails where VI–Ts negative correlation is absent (dense forests, cold-season/temperate regions, homogeneous bare surfaces), (2) ERA5_Rd biases (especially over savannas) strongly affect net radiation and ET, (3) scale/footprint mismatch between tower (~100–200 m) and 0.05° grids (~25 km^2) introduces errors, (4) MODIS data gaps (~one-third of days) require gap-filling which may reduce accuracy on cloudy days, (5) lack of soil moisture or explicit water-availability state in the algorithm can lead to overestimation of ET in energy-rich but water-limited tropical regions, (6) the method does not estimate dew-point/humidity directly and thus cannot be used immediately for Tmin->Tdew reconstructions without additional conversions and constraints.

extracted_data.name_full: Multi-step autoregressive training objective
extracted_data.brief_description: Training objective that sums prediction losses across M successive autoregressive forecast steps (M ∈ {1,2,4}) with Δt=6 h to mitigate error growth in iterative rollouts.
extracted_data.study_region_context: Global, coarse (5.625°) ERA5-based WeatherBench1 grid; no sub-regional/climate-zone-specific fitting described.
extracted_data.target_variable: All prognostic variables including near-surface temperature (tas) and specific humidity (hus) at multiple pressure levels (used jointly in multi-variable autoregressive forecasts); not targeted specifically to dew-point but relevant to humidity prediction.
extracted_data.predictors_used: Full set of prognostic variables (either 8-variable or 33-variable sets including tas and hus), constant fields (lsm, orog, lat, lon) and forcing (tisr). Not a Tmin-only method.
extracted_data.baseline_assumptions_compared: Compared against climatology baseline (temporal average over 1979–2007 training period) as lower-bound; no mention or comparison to FAO-56 Tdew≈Tmin or simple Tmin-to-Tdew rules.
extracted_data.method_model_type: Deep-learning autoregressive sequence model (ClimaX / FourCastNet / SFNO) trained with multi-step MSE loss summed across M autoregressive steps; not a statistical regression like LOESS/GAM.
extracted_data.seasonal_dayofyear_pooling: No per-day-of-year or seasonal local regression described; seasonality handled implicitly by training data spanning 1979–2007 and by using TISR as forcing; no explicit day-of-year windows or harmonic terms.
extracted_data.localization_stratification: No geographic or climate-zone stratified fitting; models trained globally on gridded data at 5.625° resolution.
extracted_data.anomaly_definition: No anomaly-based training described for predictors or targets (models are trained on z-score normalized absolute variables using global mean and std computed over training set).
extracted_data.autoregressive_or_lag_terms: Explicit autoregressive setup: models forecast next state and are rolled forward; training experiments varied M ∈ {1,2,4} autoregressive steps (Δt = 6 h). Multi-step training (M>1) reduces 10-year rollout RMSE and improves stability.
extracted_data.accuracy_metrics: Area-weighted normalized RMSE averaged across evaluated variables (tas, uas, vas, ta850, zg500) and compared to climatology RMSE; values reported qualitatively (RMSE 'close to climatology'); no numerical RMSE table in text (figures show distributions).
extracted_data.validation_design: Training: 1979–2007; validation: 2008; testing/rollout initialization: 2009–01-01 00:00 UTC; 10-year autoregressive rollouts (2009–2018). 42368 training samples (sampling 4 initial times per day). Grid-search across architectures, capacities and M; 10 random seeds per configuration.
extracted_data.reported_skill_mechanisms: Multi-step training mitigates autoregressive error growth and enhances long-term stability; geometry-aware SFNO implicitly enforces geometrical constraints allowing higher capacity without overfitting.
extracted_data.interpretation_of_broad_smoothing: Not applicable for seasonal/day-of-year pooling (no explicit broad smoothing used); implied preference for multi-step objective to reduce accumulation of short-term errors rather than temporal smoothing.
extracted_data.physical_constraints_or_qc: No explicit physical post-processing constraints (e.g., ensuring Tdew ≤ Tair or RH bounds) applied; variables normalized by global mean/std; relative humidity was omitted from one prognostic set (33-variable set minus RH).
extracted_data.failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint: No explicit reports of extremely high dew-point values, but some autoregressive rollouts 'completely degenerate' or 'explode' producing physically implausible distributions for some seeds/configurations (instability observed across variables including near-surface quantities).
extracted_data.hypothesized_failure_mechanisms: Attributed to model design and training factors: insufficient multi-step training (M=1), inappropriate model capacity (overfitting for ClimaX/FCN when too large), sensitivity to random seed, and choice of prognostic variables; SFNO more robust due to geometry-awareness. Also noted lack of explicit forcing (ocean state/greenhouse gas) can limit realism over decades.
extracted_data.climate_zone_specific_findings: No explicit per-climate-zone breakdown; however, authors note instability tied to 'noisy signals close to the poles' when model capacity increases, suggesting polar-region overfitting issues.
extracted_data.key_equations_or_parameterizations: Training loss: L_t = Σ_{m=0}^{M-1} Σ_{k=1}^{Kp} Σ_{h=1}^{H} a_h Σ_{w=1}^{W} (X_{t+mΔt} + f_θ(X_{t+mΔt}, F_{t+mΔt}, C) - X_{t+(m+1)Δt})^2. No Tmin→Tdew parameterization provided.
extracted_data.data_sources: WeatherBench1 dataset (hourly ERA5 reanalysis interpolated bilinearly to a regular 5.625° lat-lon grid, covering 1979–2018); prognostic sets include tas and hus among others. Forcing TISR computed from CMIP6 solar forcing (Matthes et al. 2017).
extracted_data.notable_limitations_caveats: Coarse spatial resolution (5.625°) may limit applicability to station-scale Tmin→Tdew approaches; models are not forced by ocean/greenhouse gas trends so cannot be expected to beat climatology; sensitivity to random seeds and prognostic variable set; no explicit physical constraints or station-level QC described.

extracted_data.name_full: Temporal-climatology baseline from training period
extracted_data.brief_description: Baseline method defined as the temporal average (climatology) over the 29-year training period (1979–2007), used as a lower-bound reference for long-term rollout RMSE comparison.
extracted_data.study_region_context: Global gridded WeatherBench1 (ERA5-derived) domain at 5.625° resolution.
extracted_data.target_variable: Same prognostic variables as models (e.g., tas, uas, vas, ta850, zg500); climatology used as benchmark for all evaluated variables including specific humidity (hus) when present.
extracted_data.predictors_used: None — climatology is the temporal mean per grid cell computed over the training period.
extracted_data.baseline_assumptions_compared: Climatology itself is the baseline; authors explicitly state they use climatology as lower-bound and do not expect models (unforced by ocean/GHG) to outperform it. No FAO-56 or Tmin-based baselines are used or compared.
extracted_data.method_model_type: Empirical temporal averaging (grid-cell mean over training years).
extracted_data.seasonal_dayofyear_pooling: Climatology computed as temporal average over entire multi-year training period (1979–2007); no explicit day-of-year smoothing/windowing described for the baseline.
extracted_data.localization_stratification: Per-grid-cell climatology (spatially local), derived from global gridded dataset.
extracted_data.anomaly_definition: Climatology is the baseline; no anomalies used for model inputs in baseline comparisons.
extracted_data.autoregressive_or_lag_terms: Not applicable for climatology baseline.
extracted_data.accuracy_metrics: Baseline RMSE computed and used to contextualize model RMSE; models that reach RMSE 'close to climatology' considered successful. Exact numeric RMSEs not tabulated in text.
extracted_data.validation_design: Climatology derived from 1979–2007 training period and compared against 10-year test period (2009–2018) rollouts.
extracted_data.reported_skill_mechanisms: Climatology acts as a stable long-term estimator since models lack realistic external forcings; used as pragmatic lower bound for 10-year unforced rollouts.
extracted_data.interpretation_of_broad_smoothing: Implicit: multi-year averaging reduces internal variability and sets a conservative benchmark; authors emphasize climatology indicates how climate changed between training and evaluation periods.
extracted_data.physical_constraints_or_qc: Not applicable beyond the underlying ERA5 QC used to produce WeatherBench1.
extracted_data.hypothesized_failure_mechanisms: Not applicable beyond caution that climatology cannot capture forced trends.
extracted_data.climate_zone_specific_findings: Climatology is computed globally per grid cell; no specific zone analysis presented.
extracted_data.key_equations_or_parameterizations: Temporal mean (climatology) over training years; no further parameterization.
extracted_data.data_sources: Computed from WeatherBench1 (ERA5-based) training years 1979–2007.
extracted_data.notable_limitations_caveats: Climatology does not capture externally forced changes (e.g., GHG, ocean state) and may incorporate interpolation artifacts from WeatherBench creation.

extracted_data.name_full: Use of specific humidity (hus) as a prognostic variable
extracted_data.brief_description: Specific humidity (hus) at multiple pressure levels (925, 850, 700, 600, 500, 250 hPa) is included in the 33-variable prognostic set and used by models to predict humidity-related fields.
extracted_data.study_region_context: Global ERA5-derived WeatherBench1 grid at 5.625° resolution.
extracted_data.target_variable: Specific humidity (hus) itself is predicted in models when included; dew point not explicitly targeted but hus is physically related to vapor pressure and dew point.
extracted_data.predictors_used: hus along with tas, winds, geopotential heights, and other atmospheric levels; not a single-Tmin predictor approach.
extracted_data.baseline_assumptions_compared: No simple physical conversion baselines (e.g., Tmin→Tdew) compared; models' hus forecasts compared indirectly via RMSE vs climatology.
extracted_data.method_model_type: Learned multivariate deep-learning autoregressive models (ClimaX/FCN/SFNO) predicting hus jointly with other prognostic variables.
extracted_data.seasonal_dayofyear_pooling: No explicit seasonal/day-of-year stratification for hus modeling; seasonality learned from full training record.
extracted_data.localization_stratification: Global gridded training; no station/local hus-specific regressions.
extracted_data.anomaly_definition: No explicit anomalies used; variables z-score normalized globally across training period.
extracted_data.autoregressive_or_lag_terms: hus is predicted inside autoregressive rollouts; training experimented with 1–4-step autoregressive objectives to reduce drift in hus forecasts.
extracted_data.accuracy_metrics: hus included in aggregated RMSEs for rollouts (figures include comparisons averaged over many variables and across seeds); no per-variable numeric table in main text for hus specifically.
extracted_data.validation_design: Same training/validation/test split as other prognostic variables; 10-year rollouts evaluated against ERA5 test period (2009–2018).
extracted_data.reported_skill_mechanisms: Including humidity prognostics can both help and harm stability depending on model architecture and capacity; larger prognostic sets destabilized some FCN/SFNO configurations while ClimaX benefited from more variables.
extracted_data.interpretation_of_broad_smoothing: Not discussed specifically for hus.
extracted_data.physical_constraints_or_qc: No humidity-specific physical post-processing (e.g., clipping, ensuring non-negativity beyond implicit DL outputs) described.
extracted_data.failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint: No direct dew-point failures reported, but instability in hus forecasts for some seeds/configurations noted (rollouts 'explode' or degenerate).
extracted_data.hypothesized_failure_mechanisms: Instability when including hus may arise from increased dimensionality/noise, capacity mismatch leading to overfitting, or inadequate training protocol for coupled humidity–temperature dynamics.
extracted_data.climate_zone_specific_findings: No explicit breakdown by climate zone for hus performance.
extracted_data.key_equations_or_parameterizations: No explicit parameterizations converting hus to dew point given; only model training loss provided.
extracted_data.data_sources: hus values extracted from ERA5 via WeatherBench1 (levels listed in Table 2).
extracted_data.notable_limitations_caveats: Authors note that adding more prognostic variables (like hus) can destabilize some architectures depending on seed and capacity; coarse resolution may smooth local humidity gradients important for dew-point estimation.

extracted_data.name_full: WeatherBench1 (ERA5) bilinear interpolation and dataset provenance
extracted_data.brief_description: WeatherBench1 is derived from ERA5 reanalysis and bilinearly interpolated to a 5.625° regular lat-lon grid; this preprocessing and coarse resolution are noted as potential limitations/artifacts.
extracted_data.study_region_context: Global gridded domain at 5.625°; therefore station-scale microclimates (e.g., Andes valleys, coastal deserts) are not resolved.
extracted_data.target_variable: All prognostic variables in WeatherBench1 (tas, hus, winds, geopotential, etc.).
extracted_data.predictors_used: Underlying ERA5 variables; authors list prognostic, constant and forcing fields used as model inputs.
extracted_data.baseline_assumptions_compared: No Tmin→Tdew baselines used; authors note climatology baseline derived from same interpolated data.
extracted_data.method_model_type: Dataset preprocessing: bilinear interpolation from ERA5 to regular grid (WeatherBench1) used as model input; not a modeling method per se but relevant to data artifacts.
extracted_data.seasonal_dayofyear_pooling: Dataset contains full diurnal/seasonal cycles across 1979–2018; no additional day-of-year pooling applied in preprocessing.
extracted_data.localization_stratification: Dataset includes land-sea mask and orography as constant fields; no station-level data provided.
extracted_data.anomaly_definition: Not applicable to interpolation step; models apply z-score normalization using global training means and stds.
extracted_data.autoregressive_or_lag_terms: Temporal resolution kept at 6-hourly Δt (models trained for 6 h steps); rollouts performed at this temporal resolution.
extracted_data.accuracy_metrics: Not directly applicable; dataset provenance influences downstream RMSE results.
extracted_data.validation_design: WeatherBench split used: 1979–2007 train, 2008 validation, 2009–2018 test; training samples count = 42368 (4 initial times per day).
extracted_data.reported_skill_mechanisms: Authors caution that bilinear interpolation and coarse resolution may limit representativeness and that results may not generalize to higher spatial resolutions.
extracted_data.interpretation_of_broad_smoothing: Bilinear interpolation and coarse grid smooth fine-scale variability, effectively applying a spatial smoothing that may reduce noise but also remove local extremes relevant to station-level dew point.
extracted_data.physical_constraints_or_qc: Underlying ERA5 QC properties apply; no additional station-level QC described. Authors removed relative humidity from one prognostic set.
extracted_data.failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint: No dew-point-specific failures attributed to interpolation, but authors flag potential interpolation artifacts as a caveat for generalization and physical realism.
extracted_data.hypothesized_failure_mechanisms: Interpolation/coarse-graining can mask local moisture gradients and cold-air pooling effects; may bias humidity fields relative to station Tmin→Tdew relationships.
extracted_data.climate_zone_specific_findings: Coarse grid cannot resolve e.g., Andes elevation contrasts or coastal desert microclimates; authors explicitly note unclear generalization to higher spatial resolutions.
extracted_data.key_equations_or_parameterizations: Bilinear interpolation method used in creating WeatherBench1 from ERA5 (Rasp et al., 2020) as documented by WeatherBench; no further equations provided here.
extracted_data.data_sources: WeatherBench1 (Rasp et al., 2020) created from ERA5 (Hersbach et al., 2020) covering 1979–2018 at hourly resolution before interpolation.
extracted_data.notable_limitations_caveats: Interpolation artifacts, coarse resolution (5.625°), and absence of station-level QC limit direct applicability to Tmin→Tdew station-scale reconstructions; authors caution on generalization to higher resolution.

extracted_data.name_full: Autoregressive rollout instability and degenerate/exploding solutions
extracted_data.brief_description: Observed failure mode where some trained models (dependent on random seed, capacity, and prognostic set) produce degenerate or exploding 10-year rollouts, producing physically implausible distributions for predicted variables.
extracted_data.study_region_context: Global ERA5-derived grid; instability sometimes traced to noisy signals near the poles but not localized to humid tropical lowlands in the paper.
extracted_data.target_variable: All prognostic variables (tas, hus, winds, geopotential); failures manifest in multiple variables simultaneously.
extracted_data.predictors_used: Failures occur across model configurations using different prognostic sets (8- and 33-variable sets) and architectures (ClimaX, FCN, SFNO).
extracted_data.baseline_assumptions_compared: Failing rollouts produce RMSE much larger than climatology baseline; climatology used to contextualize severity.
extracted_data.method_model_type: Observed across deep-learning autoregressive architectures (ClimaX, FourCastNet, SFNO) under certain hyperparameters and seeds.
extracted_data.seasonal_dayofyear_pooling: Not implicated as a remedy in the paper; failures occur despite full seasonal coverage in training data.
extracted_data.localization_stratification: No spatial stratified retraining described to address failure; failures sometimes associated with polar-region noise when capacity increases.
extracted_data.anomaly_definition: No anomaly-based mitigation described; failures occur when models trained on absolute (z-score normalized) fields.
extracted_data.autoregressive_or_lag_terms: Failure risk reduced by multi-step training (higher M) — single-step (M=1) more prone to instability; autoregressive rollout itself is the process where errors compound leading to degeneracy.
extracted_data.accuracy_metrics: Instability characterized qualitatively and via large increases in area-weighted normalized RMSE; figures show distributions and some seeds with infinite/very large RMSE (excluded from mean).
extracted_data.validation_design: Instability observed during 10-year autoregressive rollouts initialized from 2009–01-01; multiple random seeds (10) per configuration revealed seed-dependent failures.
extracted_data.reported_skill_mechanisms: Authors attribute improved robustness primarily to multi-step training and to SFNO geometry-awareness; inadequate capacity choice or too-large capacity (leading to overfitting) is implicated in failures for FCN and ClimaX.
extracted_data.interpretation_of_broad_smoothing: Not discussed; paper emphasizes architectural and training-protocol remedies (multi-step objective, appropriate capacity) rather than temporal smoothing.
extracted_data.physical_constraints_or_qc: No post hoc physical constraint enforcement described to prevent exploding variables (e.g., clipping, conservation enforcement).
extracted_data.failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint: Paper does not document explicit high dew-point (<-> extremely humid) events or >30–35°C dew points; failures are multivariate degeneracies that could, in principle, produce unphysical humidity/dew-point-like extremes but are not specifically analyzed for dew point.
extracted_data.hypothesized_failure_mechanisms: Mechanisms proposed: accumulation of autoregressive errors mitigated by multi-step training; overfitting to noisy polar signals with high-capacity non-geometry-aware models; randomness in initialization (seed sensitivity); missing external forcings (ocean state, GHG) for long-term realism.
extracted_data.climate_zone_specific_findings: Authors note noisy signals near poles and mention that some models overfit 'noisy signals close to the poles' when capacity is increased, but do not provide tropical/dry-season failure diagnostics.
extracted_data.key_equations_or_parameterizations: No special equation beyond training loss; failure diagnosis qualitative and based on RMSE and visual inspection of rollouts (timeseries and maps in appendix).
extracted_data.data_sources: Failures observed on WeatherBench1 (ERA5-derived) 5.625° dataset for 10-year rollouts (2009–2018) across multiple model configurations and random seeds.
extracted_data.notable_limitations_caveats: Authors stress that demonstrations at coarse resolution may not generalize to higher resolutions; lack of physical constraint enforcement and unforced setup (no ocean coupling) are key caveats for interpreting stability and failure modes.

extracted_data.name_full: Penman-Monteith temperature approach – dew-point estimation from Tmin with correction
extracted_data.brief_description: Estimation of actual vapour pressure (ea) for the Penman-Monteith temperature approach by assuming dew-point temperature Tdew ≈ Tmin (FAO-56 default) and introducing a calibrated temperature correction a_T so that Tdew = Tmin - a_T; coefficients calibrated annually and seasonally for the Cerrado.
extracted_data.citation_title: Improvement of reference crop evapotranspiration estimates using limited data for the Brazilian Cerrado
extracted_data.study_region_context: Brazilian Cerrado biome (tropical savannah with dry winter, Köppen class referenced via Alvares et al. 2013). Spatial extent: longitudes ~60°28'W to 41°16'48"W, latitudes ~2°19'48"S to 24°40'55"S; elevation range 0–2854 m (mean ≈ 396 m). Two seasons: wet Oct–Apr and dry May–Sept. Dataset: 132 stations (82 AWS + 50 conventional) 2000–2020; calibration 2000–2014, validation 2015–2020.
extracted_data.target_variable: Actual vapour pressure ea (kPa) computed from dew-point temperature Tdew (°C) via saturation vapour pressure; dew-point is the reconstructed variable (Tdew in °C).
extracted_data.predictors_used: Primary predictor: daily Tmin (T_min). Additional inputs used elsewhere in PMT: Tmax, Tavg, temperature range (Tmax-Tmin) for Rs estimation, assumed or calibrated wind speed u2 when missing (default 2.0 m/s or calibrated value). No use of precipitation, soil moisture, or explicit advection fields in the PMT calibration; solar radiation Rs was estimated from temperature range using Hargreaves formulation when missing.
extracted_data.baseline_assumptions_compared: FAO-56 default Tdew = Tmin (a_T = 0) and world-average wind speed u2 = 2.0 m s^-1; paper compares model performance using original FAO defaults versus coefficients calibrated for the Cerrado (annual and seasonally).
extracted_data.method_model_type: Deterministic FAO56 PM temperature approach with empirical adjustments: Tdew parameterized as Tdew = Tmin - a_T. Calibration of scalar parameters (a_T and u2 among others) by nonlinear least-squares minimization (Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm) applied to biome-wide training set (single set of coefficients for the entire Cerrado) and also stratified by season (wet/dry). No use of machine-learning time-series models for dewpoint; Rs estimated by Hargreaves (empirical) when needed.
extracted_data.seasonal_dayofyear_pooling: Seasonal stratification only: two-season split (wet Oct–Apr; dry May–Sept). Also evaluated annual single calibration. No day-of-year kernel smoothing, moving-window widths, harmonic terms, or explicit per-day-of-year regressions reported. Monthly performance was assessed post-hoc, but no per-month model fitting beyond wet/dry.
extracted_data.localization_stratification: A single parameter set calibrated for the entire Cerrado was preferred (practical stakeholder recommendation). The authors evaluated station-wise performance for diagnostics but did not fit station-specific models; they tested seasonal (wet/dry) parameter sets in addition to the annual set. Clustering or sub-regional parameterizations were discussed (cited Ferreira et al. 2019) but not adopted here; station-wise NSE maps were produced to show spatial variation.
extracted_data.anomaly_definition: No use of anomalies or detrended anomalies for dewpoint estimation reported. Calibration used raw daily values (no explicit anomaly-based training).
extracted_data.autoregressive_or_lag_terms: No autoregressive (lag) terms or persistence models for dew-point/humidity were used or reported.
extracted_data.accuracy_metrics: Metrics reported are for ETo (which depends on ea): PBIAS, MAE, RMSE, NSE. For PMT (using calibrated parameters) reported validation performance: MAE (before calibration) ≈ 0.74 mm d^-1; annual calibration reduced MAE by ~17%; PMT RMSE (annual calibrated) = 0.80 mm d^-1; NSE (annual) = 0.58 (seasonal NSE = 0.59). Note: these are ETo error metrics, not direct Tdew/ea error metrics. The paper also reports calibration values for a_T and u2 (see key_equations_or_parameterizations).
extracted_data.validation_design: Temporal split validation: calibration on 2000–2014 (~70% of data), validation on 2015–2020 (~30%). Dataset comprised 132 INMET stations (82 AWS, 50 CWS). Stations with <10 years of observations excluded. Performance reported for whole validation set, monthly periods, and spatially by station.
extracted_data.reported_skill_mechanisms: Physical/statistical explanations given for why adjusting Tdew away from Tmin improves PMT: in humid conditions daytime absolute humidity (from evapotranspiration and humidification) can be higher than nighttime humidity so Tdew > Tmin (requires negative a_T), while in drier seasons Tmin tends to approach Tdew (small positive a_T) if wind is calm. Wind speed and seasonality of humidity influence the Tmin–Tdew relationship; thus seasonally-tuned a_T can reduce bias. The authors emphasize that lack of wind and RH inputs constrains skill, and that improving solar radiation representation is crucial for temperature-based ETo methods.
extracted_data.interpretation_of_broad_smoothing: Authors implicitly prefer broad seasonal pooling (single annual or two-season coefficients) for practicality and because station-level clustering did not show meaningful improvements for the Cerrado; they note seasonal parametrization reduced monthly systematic bias but provided only small overall metric improvements. No explicit argument for day-of-year smoothing bandwidths; rationale for broad pooling includes sample size, operational simplicity, and the Cerrado's predominant tropical savanna climate with strong seasonality.
extracted_data.physical_constraints_or_qc: Extensive QC before modeling: removed impossible values (infinite, negative wind), enforced Tmin ≤ Tmax, removed SH or Rs values above physically possible limits, bounded RH to 5–100% (values outside removed), compared Rs to clear-sky Rs (Allen 1996) and removed periods with shifts, visually screened for homogeneity; stations with <10 years excluded. No additional clipping of reconstructed Tdew reported, but standard psychrometric conversion used: e_a = 0.6108 * exp(17.27*Tdew/(Tdew+237.3)).
extracted_data.failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint: The paper does not report instances of model-produced physically implausible extreme dew points (e.g., >30–35°C) from PMT. It does report that the FAO assumption Tdew = Tmin can be wrong: Tdew is often higher than Tmin in humid (wet-season) conditions (negative a_T), and opposite in some semi-arid contexts; this mismatch causes bias in ETo. No explicit report of supersaturation or extreme-unphysical dewpoint artifacts in their calibrated PMT.
extracted_data.hypothesized_failure_mechanisms: Physical mechanisms discussed: daytime evapotranspiration and humidification raising daytime absolute humidity so that nighttime Tmin can be less than Tdew; wind speed and advection affecting the exchange and raising the Priestley–Taylor alpha in dry/advection-prone conditions; cloudiness and solar radiation variance controlling Tmin–Tdew coupling. Data/model artifact mechanisms discussed: poor Rs estimation from empirical temperature-based Rs models limiting PMT skill; satellite/reanalysis products may require bias correction/adjustment to reference-site conditions; discontinuities and inhomogeneities in station data can affect calibration. Sensor wetting or ventilation issues are not specifically reported, but general station QC and homogeneity screening were applied.
extracted_data.climate_zone_specific_findings: Season-specific calibration produced different a_T: wet season (Oct–Apr) a_T = -0.93 °C (Tdew often > Tmin), dry season (May–Sept) a_T = 0.57 °C (Tdew slightly < Tmin). The annual (whole-period) calibrated a_T = -0.42 °C, implying Tdew generally higher than Tmin across the Cerrado when pooled. Central Cerrado stations showed somewhat lower method performance (station-wise NSE maps). Wind speed and RH differences between wet/dry seasons (wet RH avg ≈ 73.6%, dry ≈ 59.9%) were linked to varying Tmin–Tdew relations and model performance.
extracted_data.key_equations_or_parameterizations: Primary dew-point relation used and calibrated in paper: (Eq.2) e_a = 0.6108 * exp(17.27 * Tdew / (Tdew + 237.3)) ; (Eq.3) Tdew = Tmin - a_T. Calibrated a_T values: annual a_T = -0.42 °C; wet-season a_T = -0.93 °C; dry-season a_T = 0.57 °C. Calibrated mean wind speed used when missing: u2 (annual) = 1.23 m s^-1 (original FAO default = 2.0 m s^-1); seasonal u2: wet = 1.17 m s^-1, dry = 1.31 m s^-1. Rs estimation used Eq.4 (Hargreaves): Rs = k_Rs * sqrt(Tmax - Tmin) * Ra, with calibrated k_Rs annual = 0.159 (orig 0.16), wet = 0.155, dry = 0.165.
extracted_data.data_sources: INMET (Brazilian National Institute of Meteorology) station network: 82 automatic weather stations (AWS) and 50 conventional weather stations (CWS). Daily values derived from 2000–2020; hourly AWS aggregated to daily. Stations adhere to WMO instrument/observation guidance. Calibration period 2000–2014; validation 2015–2020. Authors mention satellite data and reanalysis as possible alternatives for gaps but note they may require bias correction.
extracted_data.notable_limitations_caveats: Authors caution that PMT and other temperature-based methods are limited by poor solar radiation estimation and absence of direct RH and wind inputs; seasonal calibration produced only minor improvements in many methods because they cannot capture dynamics driven by missing variables (wind speed, RH). Calibration uses a single biome-wide parameter set for practicality but may mask local heterogeneity; clustering/station-wise parametrization was discussed but not beneficial for this region. Reported error metrics are for ETo (dependent variable) rather than direct Tdew/ea reconstruction errors; direct dew-point reconstruction accuracy is not reported numerically.

extracted_data.name_full: FAO-56 default dew-point assumption: Tdew ≈ Tmin
extracted_data.brief_description: FAO-56 recommends, when relative humidity is unavailable, to approximate dew-point temperature by the daily minimum air temperature (Tdew = Tmin); this paper treats that assumption as a baseline and tests a scalar correction a_T.
extracted_data.citation_title: Improvement of reference crop evapotranspiration estimates using limited data for the Brazilian Cerrado
extracted_data.study_region_context: Applied as a general baseline for the Cerrado (tropical savannah with dry winter); authors investigate its adequacy in humid vs dry seasons and calibrate deviations for the Cerrado.
extracted_data.target_variable: Dew-point temperature Tdew (°C) and derived actual vapour pressure ea (kPa).
extracted_data.predictors_used: Baseline assumes only Tmin is used to approximate Tdew (i.e., no extra predictors).
extracted_data.baseline_assumptions_compared: Directly compared to calibrated correction (Tdew = Tmin - a_T) and discussed against climatological/seasonal behaviour of humidity; world-average wind speed and other FAO defaults are also used as baseline comparisons.
extracted_data.method_model_type: Baseline is a simple equality assumption (Tdew = Tmin). The paper evaluates bias introduced by this assumption and fits a single scalar correction a_T using least-squares against PM-ETo-derived ea.
extracted_data.seasonal_dayofyear_pooling: Authors examine the FAO assumption across seasons (wet vs dry) and find systematic seasonal deviations (calibrated a_T differs by season). No day-of-year smoothing beyond comparing monthly biases.
extracted_data.localization_stratification: Baseline applied uniformly; authors test whether a single biome-wide correction is adequate and show seasonal stratification improves monthly bias even if not large overall.
extracted_data.anomaly_definition: Not applicable — baseline is raw Tmin equality, not anomaly-based.
extracted_data.autoregressive_or_lag_terms: None.
extracted_data.accuracy_metrics: Not reported directly for Tdew; baseline effects evaluated indirectly via ETo metrics (e.g., bias in PMT estimates when using FAO defaults). Authors report that using FAO defaults led to larger PBIAS and MAE which are reduced after calibration (percent reductions reported).
extracted_data.validation_design: As per paper: calibration on 2000–2014 and validation on 2015–2020 over 132 stations; baseline (a_T=0) performance compared to calibrated a_T during validation.
extracted_data.reported_skill_mechanisms: Authors note FAO equality assumption is often violated: in humid regions and wet season Tdew can be higher than Tmin (so baseline underestimates vapour pressure), while in drier seasons Tmin may be closer to Tdew. The coupling depends on wind speed, evapotranspiration-driven humidification, and cloudiness.
extracted_data.interpretation_of_broad_smoothing: Seasonal correction (wet/dry) was shown to reduce monthly bias compared to annual baseline; the authors recommend seasonal tuning when possible but note limited overall gains given missing meteorological variables.
extracted_data.physical_constraints_or_qc: Paper enforces physical QC before any use: RH bounded 5–100%, Tmin ≤ Tmax, removal of unrealistic Rs/SH, comparison of Rs to clear-sky; no additional constraints applied to baseline equality itself.
extracted_data.failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint: Paper does not document explicit extreme/unphysical dewpoint values resulting from the FAO baseline, but highlights that FAO assumption can produce systematic underestimation of vapour pressure in humid/wet-season conditions (when Tdew > Tmin).
extracted_data.hypothesized_failure_mechanisms: Physical causes for the FAO baseline failure: daytime evapotranspiration raising daytime absolute humidity so nighttime Tmin < Tdew; seasonal variations in wind/advection and cloudiness decouple Tmin from dewpoint. Data/model artifacts: using default world-average wind or poor Rs estimates compounds errors in PMT when relying on the FAO Tmin approximation.
extracted_data.climate_zone_specific_findings: For Cerrado: wet-season bias consistent with Tdew > Tmin (calibrated a_T negative), dry-season bias smaller and sometimes with Tdew < Tmin (a_T positive). Reported a_T: annual -0.42°C, wet -0.93°C, dry +0.57°C.
extracted_data.key_equations_or_parameterizations: Baseline relation: Tdew = Tmin (FAO-56 default). Calibrated alternative: Tdew = Tmin - a_T with reported a_T values (annual and seasonal) as above. ea computed from Tdew via saturation vapour pressure equation (0.6108*exp(17.27*Tdew/(Tdew+237.3))).
extracted_data.data_sources: Same INMET station network and temporal split as other analyses in paper (2000–2020; calibration 2000–2014; validation 2015–2020).
extracted_data.notable_limitations_caveats: Authors emphasize that FAO default may be regionally biased (especially in humid/tropical areas) and that using a calibrated scalar correction reduces bias; however, calibration relies on good-quality reference PM-ETo which itself requires other inputs. They note that the absence of RH and wind inputs limits correction capability.

extracted_data.name_full: Hargreaves-Samani empirical solar radiation estimator (Rs from temperature range)
extracted_data.brief_description: Empirical estimate of daily global solar radiation Rs from temperature range: Rs = k_Rs * sqrt(Tmax - Tmin) * Ra; used in PMT and HS when sunshine or Rs observations are missing and calibrated here for the Cerrado.
extracted_data.citation_title: Improvement of reference crop evapotranspiration estimates using limited data for the Brazilian Cerrado
extracted_data.study_region_context: Applied to the Cerrado biome (tropical savannah) as the main pathway to provide Rs when only temperature data are available; seasonal calibration assessed.
extracted_data.target_variable: Global solar radiation Rs (MJ m^-2 d^-1) estimated from temperature range and extraterrestrial radiation Ra.
extracted_data.predictors_used: Predictors: Tmax, Tmin (temperature range) and station latitude/day-of-year via Ra. No cloud cover or satellite radiation used for this Rs estimator in the main workflow.
extracted_data.baseline_assumptions_compared: Original Hargreaves k_Rs = 0.16 (inland default) versus calibrated k_Rs for Cerrado: annual 0.159, wet 0.155, dry 0.165. Authors compare original vs calibrated coefficients and quantify Rs estimation errors.
extracted_data.method_model_type: Simple empirical formula (Hargreaves 1985) with a scalar k_Rs tuned by nonlinear least-squares (Levenberg–Marquardt) annually and seasonally for the biome.
extracted_data.seasonal_dayofyear_pooling: Calibration performed for entire period (annual) and for two-season stratification (wet/dry). No per-day-of-year smoothing or moving-window fitting reported.
extracted_data.localization_stratification: Single biome-wide k_Rs (and seasonal k_Rs) calibrated; station-wise diagnostics reported but no station-specific k_Rs applied as the recommended operational choice.
extracted_data.anomaly_definition: Not applicable (raw temperature range used).
extracted_data.autoregressive_or_lag_terms: None.
extracted_data.accuracy_metrics: For Rs estimation using Eq.4 with seasonal calibration: MAE = 2.88 MJ m^-2 d^-1, RMSE = 3.63 MJ m^-2 d^-1, NSE = 0.46 (validation). These Rs errors are cited as a major limitation for temperature-based ETo methods (PMT and HS).
extracted_data.validation_design: Same temporal calibration/validation split as other methods (2000–2014 calibration; 2015–2020 validation) across the 132 INMET stations; performance assessed at national/biome scale and monthly.
extracted_data.reported_skill_mechanisms: Authors argue Rs is the variable most correlated to ETo (wet-season Rs correlation to ETo = 0.94) and that poor Rs estimation propagates into large ETo errors for temperature-based methods. Improving Rs estimation from limited data is thus a priority.
extracted_data.interpretation_of_broad_smoothing: Seasonal calibration changed k_Rs slightly and reduced bias, but broad (annual) calibration already produced k_Rs near FAO default; authors highlight that more sophisticated Rs estimation methods (cited Fan et al. 2018 and others) could substantially improve PMT/HS performance.
extracted_data.physical_constraints_or_qc: Rs series QC included comparison to clear-sky Rs (Allen 1996) and removal of periods with shifts; unrealistic Rs/SH values were removed prior to calibration. No physical enforcement within the Hargreaves formula beyond positive Rs and climatological Ra.
extracted_data.failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint: Not directly applicable to Rs estimator, but the authors state that poor Rs estimates propagate into ETo bias; no explicit Rs-driven unphysical dewpoint artifacts are reported.
extracted_data.hypothesized_failure_mechanisms: Limitations cause: empirical Rs from temperature fails in humid/cloudy periods and has higher variance in wet season due to cloudiness and rainfall, causing degraded Rs estimates. Data artifacts (shifts, inhomogeneities) and coarse empirical form (no cloud/precipitation predictors) are flagged. Authors note alternative methods in the literature outperform the traditional Hargreaves formulation.
extracted_data.climate_zone_specific_findings: Calibrated k_Rs values vary slightly by season (wet 0.155, dry 0.165) and coastal stations tended to require slightly higher k_Rs although authors still recommend biome-wide values for practicality.
extracted_data.key_equations_or_parameterizations: Hargreaves solar radiation estimator (Eq.4): Rs = k_Rs * sqrt(Tmax - Tmin) * Ra. Calibrated k_Rs (Cerrado): annual = 0.159; wet-season = 0.155; dry-season = 0.165. Original FAO inland recommendation = 0.16.
extracted_data.data_sources: Rs ground measurements from AWS (hourly aggregated to daily) where available; otherwise Rs estimated via Hargreaves from Tmax/Tmin and Ra. Rs QC used clear-sky comparison (Allen 1996). Same INMET station network used for calibration/validation (2000–2020).
extracted_data.notable_limitations_caveats: Authors underscore that the Hargreaves Rs estimator produced poor performance (NSE = 0.46, RMSE = 3.63 MJ m^-2 d^-1) for this humid-seasonally-variable biome and that this deficiency constrains temperature-based ETo methods. They recommend exploring other empirical Rs estimators or satellite/reanalysis with bias correction.

potentially_relevant_new_papers.paper_title: Computing FAO56 reference grass evapotranspiration PM-ET _{3} from temperature with focus on solar radiation
Assessing integrity of weather data for reference evapotranspiration estimation
Evaluation and development of temperature-based empirical models for estimating daily global solar radiation in humid regions
