metadata.title: Improving the Accuracy of Subseasonal Forecasting of China Precipitation With a Machine Learning Approach

tldr.text: This work introduces the machine learning method proposed by Hwang et al. in 2019 to predict the precipitation in China 2–6 weeks in advance and shows that the subseasonal prediction of China precipitation should be benefited from the MultiLLR model.

metadata.abstract: Precipitation change, which is closely related to drought and flood disasters in China, affects billions of people every year, and the demand for subseasonal forecasting of precipitation is even more urgent. Subseasonal forecasting, which is more difficult than weather forecasting, however, has remained as a blank area in meteorological service for a long period of time. To improve the accuracy of subseasonal forecasting of China precipitation, this work introduces the machine learning method proposed by Hwang et al. in 2019 to predict the precipitation in China 2–6 weeks in advance. The authors used a non-linear regression model called local linear regression together with multitask feature election (MultiLLR) model and chosen 21 meteorological elements as candidate predictors to integrate diverse meteorological observation data. This method automatically eliminates irrelevant predictors so as to establish the forecast equations using multitask feature selection process. The experiments demonstrate that the pressure and Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO) are the most important physical factors. The average prediction skill is 0.11 during 2011–2016, and there are seasonal differences in forecasting skills, evidenced by higher forecast skills of winter and spring seasons than summer and autumn seasons. The proposed method can provide effective and indicative guidance for the subseasonal prediction of precipitation in China. By adding another three factors, Arctic Oscillation (AO) index, Western North Pacific Monsoon (WNPM) index and Western North Pacific Subtropical High (WNPSH) index into the MultiLLR model, the authors find that AO can improve the forecast skill of China precipitation to the maximum extent from 0.11 to 0.13, followed by WNPSH. Moreover, the ensemble skill of our model and CFSv2 is 0.16. This work shows that our subseasonal prediction of China precipitation should be benefited from the MultiLLR model.

content.title: Local Linear Regression with Multitask Feature Selection (MultiLLR) model

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | MultiLLR |
| name_full | Local Linear Regression with Multitask Feature Selection (MultiLLR) model |
| brief_description | A spatially-localized regression framework that fits a separate linear model at each grid point (local linear regression) combined with a multitask backward stepwise feature-selection procedure to choose relevant predictors automatically for subseasonal (weeks 3–4) precipitation forecasting. |
| citation_title | Improving subseasonal forecasting in the western U.S. with machine learning |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | China (domain: 14.75°N–55.75°N, 69.75°E–139.75°E). Results reported for whole-country and subregions (Yangtze River basin, Southeastern China, Central/Northern/Northeast China). Seasonal stratification into winter, spring (Win-Spr) and summer, autumn (Sum-Aut); no Köppen classes or elevation bands explicitly used. |
| target_variable | Two-week total precipitation (forecast target: sum of ensuing 14 days). NOTE: This study does NOT perform dew-point (Tdew) reconstruction; relative humidity (sigma level 0.995) and 2 m temperature are used as predictors but dew point is not reconstructed. |
| predictors_used | 21 candidate predictors including: 2 m temperature, relative humidity at sigma level 0.995, surface pressure, geopotential height PCs at 10 hPa, sea ice concentration, Pacific SST PCs, CFSv2 total precipitation (forecast), MJO phase/amplitude, MEI, indices AO, WNPM, WNPSH1, WNPSH2, plus lagged ('shift x') and anomalous ('anom') variants of some predictors and an intercept ('ones'). Predictors were interpolated to 1°×1° grid. (Only Tmin-specific dew-point predictors like Tmin→Tdew formulae are NOT used here.) |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | Compared against dynamical model CFSv2 operational forecasts (skill ~0.11). Also compared MultiLLR variants: 21-index baseline, 21-index+AO, 21-index+WNPM, 21-index+WNPSH; ensemble (equal-weight) of 21-index+AO MultiLLR with CFSv2 (skill improvement to 0.16). Climatology is used to compute anomalies for predictors/skill (daily climatology 1980–2010 or 1981–2010) but no FAO-56 Tdew≈Tmin or explicit dew-point climatology baseline is evaluated. |
| method_model_type | Local linear regression fit independently at each grid point (LLR) combined with multitask backward stepwise feature selection (MultiLLR). Also tested AutoKNN analog method (local linear regression with 20 nearest historical analog dates). Details: candidate regressors include intercept, anomalies, lagged ('shift x') versions; feature selection based on forecast performance using spatial cosine similarity. |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | Seasonality handled via anomalies relative to daily climatology (anom suffix) computed over 1980–2010 (predictor anomalies) and removal of climatological annual cycle over 1981–2010 for skill calculation. Predictors (except MJO) averaged over ensuing 2 weeks to match the 14-day precipitation target. No explicit moving-window LOESS/DOY kernel bandwidths reported. |
| localization_stratification | Localization achieved by fitting regression coefficients separately at each grid point (per-grid LLR). Multitask feature selection pools information spatially using spatial cosine similarity to evaluate candidate predictors, but no explicit climate-zone or elevation-band stratification was reported. |
| anomaly_definition | Predictor anomalies (suffix 'anom') are defined as departures from daily climatology computed over 1980–2010 (paper text). For forecast-skill computation anomalies were obtained by removing the climatological annual cycle during 1981–2010 (paper uses this baseline for Y and Ŷ when computing spatial cosine similarity). |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | The candidate regressors include lagged versions indicated by 'shift x' (hysteresis characteristic from previous x days based on data update timing), i.e., predictors with explicit lags; however the paper does not report explicit autoregressive terms on the predictand (precipitation) such as P(t-1) or modeled AR(p) on residuals. AutoKNN experiment uses historical-date analogs (20 dates) rather than AR coefficients. |
| accuracy_metrics | Forecast skill measured by spatial cosine similarity between observed and predicted anomalies. Reported values: average skill across 2011–2016 = 0.11 (21-index model); 21-index+AO = 0.13; CFSv2 = 0.11; ensemble (21-index+AO + CFSv2 equal weight) = 0.16. Seasonal: winter skill > 0.21, summer skill ≈ 0.0, autumn and spring intermediate. AutoKNN gave negative skill. No RMSE/MAE/Bias or dew-point-specific metrics are reported in this paper. |
| validation_design | Forecasted 26 target dates per year (every 2 weeks) for 2011–2016 → 156 forecasts. For each forecast date the training range spans from the first year when all selected predictor data are available up to the year of the target date. Evaluation across high-skill vs low-skill years and by seasons (Win-Spr vs Sum-Aut). Predictors and reanalysis interpolated to 1°×1°. No station-level holdout or cross-validated dew-point reconstruction experiments (study focused on gridded precipitation forecasting). |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | Authors attribute skill to teleconnection/large-scale drivers and land/ocean influences: MJO and surface pressure (cold surge) identified as important predictors; AO and WNPSH also improve skill (AO most helpful). Physical mechanisms invoked include modulation of southern-branch trough (SBT) and middle-east jet stream (MEJS), northward moisture transport/convergence, and intraseasonal modulation of convection (MJO). Soil moisture, SST, sea ice, and land surface processes are cited in intro as potential sources of subseasonal predictability though not all were primary predictors here. |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | Predictors (except MJO) are averaged over the ensuing 2-week target period to be consistent with the 14-day precipitation sum—this broad temporal pooling is used to match target temporal scale and reduce noise. The paper also uses daily climatology anomalies (1980–2010) implying a smoothed seasonal cycle baseline; no detailed theoretical justification for broader DOY/window widths beyond matching target averaging and sample-size considerations is given. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | No explicit physical-constraint post-processing (e.g., clipping dew point to ≤ air temperature) is reported because the target is precipitation. Data handling steps include interpolation of reanalysis predictors to 1°×1° and consistency checks on predictor availability for training range. No special QC for humidity/psychrometric conversions or sensor wetting is described. |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | The paper does NOT report any failure modes related to dew-point or unrealistically high dew-point estimates (no dew-point reconstruction performed). Reported failure modes for the precipitation task: markedly low skill in summer and autumn, poor seasonal-mean prediction in Southeastern China, tendency for model to predict drought-like anomalies (negative seasonal-mean bias), and AutoKNN delivering negative skill. |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | For poor performance the authors mention (a) physical reasons: seasonality and local weather complexity (summer/autumn precipitation patterns are harder to predict), influence of teleconnection factors varying by season (WNPM was found to be a negative contributor), and possibly insufficient representation of moisture transport processes; and (b) methodological/data reasons: limitation of using only local linear regression (authors note model simplicity limits skill), insufficient/irrelevant predictors for some regions/seasons, and potential sampling/training-range limitations. No sensor wetting, Tmin biases, or reanalysis humidity artifact hypotheses are discussed in the context of dew-point extremes. |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | Performance breakdown by region/season: better representation of intraseasonal variability (ISV) and higher skill in Yangtze River and Southeastern China during Win-Spr in high-skill years; expansion of strong ISV to Central/Northern/Northeast China in Sum-Aut but model underestimates ISV there; Southeastern China seasonal-mean precipitation particularly poorly captured. No explicit comparisons by arid vs humid or high-elevation vs lowland zones; no tropical lowland dew-point-specific analyses. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | The paper provides the forecast-skill metric: forecast_skill(Y, Ŷ) = <Y, Ŷ> / (\|\|Y\|\|2 * \|\|Ŷ\|\|2) where Y are observed anomalies and Ŷ predicted anomalies. No equations or parameterizations relating Tmin to dew point (e.g., FAO-56 Tdew≈Tmin or vapor-pressure regression) appear in this paper. |
| data_sources | Observations: CN05.1 daily precipitation dataset from China National Climate Center (1961–2017). Predictors: NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis (daily 2 m temperature, relative humidity at sigma level 0.995, surface pressure, geopotential height), NOAA/ESRL MJO, MEI from Australian Bureau of Meteorology, OISST (NOAA) SST and sea-ice concentration, CFSv2 operational 6-hourly forecast precipitation (averaged to 14-day), AO from CPC; WNPM and WNPSH indices derived from reanalysis fields. Predictors interpolated to 1°×1° grid and averaged over ensuing 2 weeks. |
| notable_limitations_caveats | Authors note the MultiLLR used only local linear regression which likely limits forecast skill and suggest testing more suitable methods. Seasonal nonstationarity, limited ability to predict summer/autumn precipitation, and regional failures (Southeastern China) are highlighted. The study did not attempt dew-point reconstruction, so no dew-point-specific validation or QC is available. Training ranges vary by target date depending on predictor availability. |

metadata.title: STEAD: a high-resolution daily gridded temperature dataset for Spain
metadata.abstract:
Abstract. Using 5520 observatories covering the whole territory of
Spain (about 1 station per 90 km2 considering the whole period), a
daily gridded maximum and minimum temperature was built covering a period
from 1901 to 2014 in peninsular Spain and 1971 to 2014 in the Balearic and Canary
Islands. A comprehensive quality control was applied to the original data,
and the gaps were filled on each day and location independently. Using the
filled data series, a grid of 5 km × 5 km spatial resolution was created by
estimating daily temperatures and their corresponding uncertainties at each
grid point. Four daily temperature indices were calculated to describe the
spatial distribution of absolute maximum and minimum temperature, number of
frost days and number of summer days in Spain. The southern plateau showed
the maximum values of maximum absolute temperature and summer days, while
the minimum absolute temperature and frost days reached their maximums at
the northern plateau. The use of all the available information, the complete
quality control and the high spatial resolution of the grid allowed for an
accurate estimate of temperature that represents a precise spatial and
temporal distribution of daily temperatures in Spain. The STEAD dataset is
publicly available at https://doi.org/10.20350/digitalCSIC/8622 and can be
cited as Serrano-Notivoli et al. (2019).

content.title: STEAD: Reference-values (RVs) based local GLMM/GLM k-nearest-neighbour reconstruction method for daily Tmax/Tmin (Spanish TEmperature At Daily scale)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | STEAD (RVs-based reconstruction) |
| name_full | STEAD: Reference-values (RVs) based local GLMM/GLM k-nearest-neighbour reconstruction method for daily Tmax/Tmin (Spanish TEmperature At Daily scale) |
| brief_description | An iterative, local reconstruction and gridding method for daily maximum and minimum temperature that (i) computes rough monthly reference values with GLMMs (year as random effect), (ii) refines monthly references using GLMs on the 15 nearest neighbours plus the rough monthly RV, and (iii) computes daily reference values with GLMs on the 15 nearest daily observations plus the fine monthly RV, standardizing daily estimates to monthly means and SDs; includes an iterative deep quality control (spatio-temporal anomaly & correlation tests), gap-filling and uncertainty estimation and builds a 5 km × 5 km gridded dataset for Spain. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | Iberian Peninsula (peninsular Spain) plus Balearic and Canary Islands; mixed climates from humid Atlantic-influenced north to arid/continental southern lowlands and Mediterranean islands; complex orography including Pyrenees and Sierra Nevada with elevations from sea level to >2000 m.a.s.l.; station density ~1 station per 90 km² across study period. |
| target_variable | Daily air temperature: maximum (Tmax) and minimum (Tmin) in °C. (The paper does not reconstruct dew point, humidity, vapor pressure or RH.) |
| predictors_used | Latitude, longitude, altitude, distance-to-coast; in the multi-stage procedure: rmRV (rough monthly RV) used as covariate for fmRV, and fmRV used as covariate for dRV; local neighbourhood observations (15 nearest neighbours) used as predictors in local GLMs. Year used as random effect in the rmRV GLMM. No moisture/humidity predictors (no precipitation, radiation, cloudiness, soil moisture or reanalysis humidity) were used to reconstruct dew point or humidity because dew point was not targeted. |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | The paper does not compare any Tmin→Tdew baseline assumptions such as FAO-56 Tdew ≈ Tmin or explicit climatological dew-point baselines. It discusses and situates its method relative to alternative temperature interpolation/gridding approaches (e.g., E-OBS, Spain02, PRISM, kriging, splines) in the literature, but does not perform a direct comparison against dew-point baselines. |
| method_model_type | Multi-stage regression framework: (1) GLMM (Gaussian) per month using all stations to compute rough monthly RVs (fixed effects: lat, lon, alt, distance-to-coast; random effect: year); (2) Local GLMs per station-month using the 15 nearest neighbours plus rmRV as covariate to compute fine monthly RVs; (3) Local GLMs per station-day using 15 nearest daily observations plus fmRV to compute daily RVs; standardization of daily predictions to monthly mean and SD. Neighborhood approach is k-nearest (k=15). Uncertainty computed as standard error of prediction differences among neighbours. No geostatistical kriging or machine-learning methods used in the method itself, though the paper cites such alternatives. |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | Seasonality handled at monthly resolution: rmRV and fmRV are computed per calendar month (i.e., separate models for each month). Daily RVs use the corresponding month's fmRV as covariate and daily neighbourhood observations. No continuous day-of-year kernel smoothing or explicit moving-window bandwiths other than 'per-month' modelling and use of the 15 nearest neighbours; no explicit day-of-year bandwidth numbers beyond per-month treatment. |
| localization_stratification | Localization achieved via k-nearest-neighbour regression (k = 15) and building local GLMs for each station/month and for each station/day; the rmRV stage is global (all data) to provide regularization (year random effect), fmRV and dRV are local. No explicit climate-zone or Köppen stratification; locality captured through geographic coordinates, altitude, and distance-to-coast covariates and neighbour selection. |
| anomaly_definition | Daily differences defined as Tdif = Tobs - dRV_SD where dRV_SD is the standardized daily RV: dRV_SD = (dRV - fmRV_mean) / fmRV_SD (Eq. 4). Spatial anomalies: standardized deviation of Tdif from 15-neighbour mean/difference (Zdif_spatial). Temporal anomalies: standardized deviation of Tdif from other days of same station-month-year (Zdif_temporal). Rough and fine monthly RVs (rmRV, fmRV) serve as climatological monthly references; rmRV computed from months with complete observations and includes year as random effect to account for temporal variability. Baseline climatologies are monthly means and SDs derived from the available station data (period covered by stations; global rmRV fit uses all available data). |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | No autoregressive/time-lag (AR) terms for dew point or temperature are used; the method does not include T(t-1) or similar lagged predictors. Year is included as a random effect in rmRV (to capture interannual variability), but no explicit AR process or persistence model is implemented. |
| accuracy_metrics | Multiple metrics reported from leave-one-out cross-validation: station-aggregated Pearson correlations for mean values 0.97 (Tmax) and 0.96 (Tmin); 95th percentile Tmax r = 0.95; 5th percentile Tmin r = 0.96. Monthly mean Pearson correlation (daily obs vs estimates) averaged 0.87 (Tmax) and 0.82 (Tmin); >80% of months for Tmax and >68% for Tmin have correlation >0.8. MAE by month: TMAX ~0.61–0.84 °C (monthly values in Table 2); TMIN MAE ~0.77–0.90 °C. Elevation-stratified MAE for TMAX increases with elevation from ~0.65 to ~1.21 °C. Ratios of standard deviations (RSD) indicate some smoothing (RSD < 1 for many months). Approximately 70% of observation–estimate differences were <1 °C. Uncertainty estimates provided as standard error of neighbour prediction differences; temporal evolution of uncertainty higher early in record and decreasing after 1960s. |
| validation_design | Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV) performed by withholding each observation in turn and predicting it from the remaining data; validation at station and daily levels. Dataset: 5520 stations across Spain (peninsular: 5056 stations 1901–2014; Balearic: 124 stations 1971–2014; Canary: 340 stations 1971–2014). Validation includes monthly aggregates, percentile extremes (95th Tmax, 5th Tmin), elevation-stratified analyses, and monthly correlation frequency plots. |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | Authors attribute skill to (a) using all available observations (not only the longest series) improving representation, (b) three-stage design combining global regularization (rmRV) with local adaptivity (fmRV,dRV) to capture local spatial features while avoiding overfitting/excessive spatial variability, and (c) inclusion of distance-to-coast, altitude and geographic coordinates which capture continentality and orographic effects. They argue local regression plus monthly temporal structure better retains local daily variability than purely global smoothing approaches. |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | The paper explicitly uses a two-scale smoothing/regularization strategy: a broadly smoothed rmRV (global GLMM per month) is included as a covariate in the local fmRV to prevent excessive spatial variability and erroneous extrapolation when using purely local models; authors note this balances local representativeness vs statistical robustness. They discuss the arbitrary choice of k=15 neighbours and trade-offs: more neighbours -> less local representativeness but more robustness; fewer neighbours -> more local detail but risk of extrapolation/noise. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | Comprehensive QC applied: initial QC removed physically impossible values (Tmax≥50 °C or Tmax≤−30 °C; Tmin≥40 °C or Tmin≤−35 °C), months with <3 days, months with zero sd, duplicated sequences; deep QC iteratively removes suspect data based on low/negative correlation with dRV (COR ≤ 0 or ZCOR extreme with p < 0.001) and spatial/temporal anomaly tests (Zdif_spatial and Zdif_temporal) with threshold α < 1e-4. After QC, gaps filled using RVs. Uncertainty per grid cell/day computed as standard error of prediction differences among 15 neighbours. No dew-point- or RH-specific physical constraints (e.g., Tdew ≤ Tair) are discussed because dew point is not reconstructed. |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | None |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | For temperature reconstruction, authors identify likely failure modes and data issues: (a) sparse station coverage and higher inter-station distances (especially early 20th century) increase uncertainty and can produce poor estimates; (b) extrapolation in geographic/altitudinal/distance-to-coast space when local neighbours are not representative can produce unrealistic values; (c) coding/transcription errors, repeated sequences, duplicated months or shifted dates in station records (detected and removed by deep QC) can produce spurious extremes; (d) arbitrary modelling choices (e.g., k=15) can affect balance between local detail and smoothness; (e) high-elevation areas and small islands have fewer stations and higher uncertainty leading to larger errors. The paper does not discuss sensor wetting, ventilation artifacts, reanalysis humidity biases, or dew-point specific measurement errors. |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | Performance and patterns vary with elevation and region: higher MAE and uncertainty at high elevations (>1300 m) and in the earliest decades due to sparse stations; northern (Atlantic-influenced) half shows stronger orographic influence and differing Tmin/Tmax patterns versus southern continental lowlands where Tmax and number of summer days are highest; Balearic and Canary Islands exhibit higher uncertainty in some indices due to few stations and local variability. No explicit Köppen-zone stratified performance metrics are provided. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | Key model and standardization equations used in the method: (1) rmRV GLMM: y ~ N(X β + Z b, σ^2), b ~ N(0, G) (Eq. 1); (2) local fmRV GLM: y' ~ N(X' β', ε) (Eq. 2); (3) daily dRV GLM: y'' ~ N(X'' β'', σ''^2) (Eq. 3); (4) daily standardization: dRV_SD_{i,d,m,y} = (dRV_{i,d,m,y} - fmRV_mean_{i,m,y}) / fmRV_SD_{i,m,y} (Eq. 4); (5) gridded standardization: GdRV_SD = (GdRV - GfmRV_mean) / GfmRV_SD (Eq. 9). No simple Tmin→Tdew parameterization or psychrometric equations are provided because dew point is not estimated in this study. |
| data_sources | 5520 in-situ daily station series provided by the Spanish Meteorological Agency (AEMET) and the Spanish Ministry of Environment and Agriculture (MAGRAMA); peninsular Spain coverage 1901–2014 (5056 stations), Balearic & Canary Islands 1971–2014 (124 and 340 stations respectively). Output gridded product at 5 km × 5 km resolution. Internal covariates (lat, lon, altitude, distance-to-coast) computed per grid cell. |
| notable_limitations_caveats | Authors note arbitrary choices (e.g., k=15 neighbours) that affect representativeness/robustness, higher uncertainty in early decades due to sparse observations, some smoothing of variability (RSD < 1) indicating reduced variance relative to observations, potential poorer performance at high elevations and small islands due to fewer stations, and quality-control thresholds chosen based on experience (not fully objective). The study does not address dew-point/humidity reconstruction and therefore does not evaluate Tmin→Tdew assumptions or dew-point-specific failure modes. |

metadata.title: An Environmental Data Set for Vector-Borne Disease Modeling and Epidemiology

tldr.text: Methods to assemble high-resolution gridded time series data sets of air temperature, relative humidity, land temperature, and rainfall for low- and middle-income areas are described and tested; and significant differences in temporal and spatial heterogeneity relevant to vector-borne disease modeling are observed.

metadata.abstract: Understanding the environmental conditions of disease transmission is important in the study of vector-borne diseases. Low- and middle-income countries bear a significant portion of the disease burden; but data about weather conditions in those countries can be sparse and difficult to reconstruct. Here, we describe methods to assemble high-resolution gridded time series data sets of air temperature, relative humidity, land temperature, and rainfall for such areas; and we test these methods on the island of Madagascar. Air temperature and relative humidity were constructed using statistical interpolation of weather station measurements; the resulting median 95th percentile absolute errors were 2.75°C and 16.6%. Missing pixels from the MODIS11 remote sensing land temperature product were estimated using Fourier decomposition and time-series analysis; thus providing an alternative to the 8-day and 30-day aggregated products. The RFE 2.0 remote sensing rainfall estimator was characterized by comparing it with multiple interpolated rainfall products, and we observed significant differences in temporal and spatial heterogeneity relevant to vector-borne disease modeling.

content.title: Kriging-based dew point interpolation with altitude lapse-rate correction and Fourier-seasonal anomaly kriging (Chabot-Couture et al. 2014)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Chabot-Couture dew‑point/RH kriging |
| name_full | Kriging-based dew point interpolation with altitude lapse-rate correction and Fourier-seasonal anomaly kriging (Chabot-Couture et al. 2014) |
| brief_description | A method to build daily gridded dew point and relative-humidity maps by (1) removing seasonal harmonics (0–3× yearly) from station time series to form anomalies, (2) fitting day-of-year semi-variograms (sill and half-correlation distance) across 30 years, (3) kriging zero-altitude-equivalent dew point, and (4) reintroducing altitude using a day-of-year lapse rate; RH is computed from gridded T and Tdew using the August–Roche–Magnus formula. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | Primary test region: Madagascar (tropical island; mix of humid lowlands, eastern moist forests, drier western interior, and mountainous interior); broader context: Africa (stations across Africa used for method and error mapping). Periods: station data 1981–2010 (Madagascar cross-validation), RFE rainfall 2001–2010; referenced WorldClim climate normals (1950–2000 baseline). Elevation considered explicitly via lapse rates; method notes differences between lowlands and high elevations and seasonal dry vs wet seasons. |
| target_variable | Dew-point temperature (T_d, °C) and Relative Humidity (RH, %). RH computed from T and T_d via August–Roche–Magnus approximation. |
| predictors_used | Primary predictors: observed station dew point and air temperature time series (GSOD network). Supporting predictors/covariates: elevation (altitude) via derived dew-point lapse rate (day-of-year dependent), WorldClim daily climate-normal temperature surface (adds systematic/mean field), Fourier-seasonal components (0,1,2,3×year) removed to form anomalies, spatial distance kernels (semi-variogram) for kriging; for land-surface-temperature completion they used temporal autocorrelation (pixel-wise) and regional daily-average anomaly as additional weight. The method does not use Tmin alone as predictor; it uses station T_d measurements when available. |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | Compared interpolation results against the supporting climate layer (WorldClim) as the mean offset; authors note that WorldClim climate-layer error (~<1°C) produces a systematic bias in air temperature estimates. The paper also cites literature recommending Tmin as an acceptable proxy when Tdew is unavailable (Kimball et al. 1997) but does not adopt Tmin-only baselines itself. No explicit comparison to FAO-56 Tdew≈Tmin is reported in this paper. |
| method_model_type | Spatial statistical interpolation: simple kriging of day-to-day anomalies (anomalies derived by subtracting orthogonalized Fourier harmonics 0–3× yearly). Variogram functional form used: γ(d) = γ(∞) (1 - 1/(1-(d/λ)^2)) with day-of-year-specific fits. Dew point: station measurements corrected to zero-altitude using a region-specific, day-of-year lapse rate (derived from 30 years of (altitude, dew point) pairs), kriged at zero-altitude, then altitude effect added back. Temporal completion for MODIS LST used temporal kriging with a fitted autocorrelation (power-law) and a linear combination with regional daily anomaly weighted by remaining variance. Smoothing of variogram parameters via median and mean 31‑day sliding windows. No explicit machine‑learning models used; algorithmic, geostatistical approach. |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | Seasonality removed by Fourier subtraction of constant plus 1×, 2×, 3× yearly harmonics (orthogonalized over valid measurements). Semi-variogram parameters (sill and half-correlation distance) fit independently for each day-of-year across 30 years of station pairs, then smoothed by two passes: median in a 31-day sliding window followed by a 31-day moving average; dew-point lapse rate day-of-year curve smoothed similarly (31-day median then 31-day average). Land-surface STD calculated with a 31-day weighted window (weights w(t)=1-\|t/16\|^3). |
| localization_stratification | Localization via (a) region selection for lapse-rate derivation (region should contain sufficient stations without encompassing very different climates), (b) day-of-year specific variogram fitting across stations within the region, and (c) altitude adjustment using a region-wide, day-of-year dew-point lapse rate. Spatial heterogeneity handled by kriging weights derived from fitted semi-variograms; no explicit climate-zone classification (e.g., Koppen) used, though authors discuss differing station densities and climate behaviour across Africa and Madagascar. |
| anomaly_definition | Anomalies = station time-series minus seasonal signal where seasonality = orthogonalized Fourier harmonics (0th, 1st, 2nd, 3rd annual harmonics) computed over valid observations. For land-surface temperature anomalies they also standardized by seasonally-varying STD to obtain zero mean, unit std 'normalized-departure' time series. |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | Explicit autoregressive/lag modeling used for MODIS land surface temperature temporal completion: pixel-wise autocorrelation functions fitted (power-law), and only valid measurements within the maximum useful lag (lag until autocorr becomes negative) were included in temporal kriging. No explicit AR terms (T_d(t-1), etc.) are reported for station dew point or air temperature kriging; interpolation is spatial kriging of daily anomalies rather than time-series AR modeling. |
| accuracy_metrics | Dew point (Madagascar cross-validation, medians across 26 stations): daily median bias = -0.177°C; median MAE = 1.25°C; median RMSE = 1.64°C; median 95th-percentile absolute error = 3.32°C. 10-day median bias = -0.289°C; 10-day 95th percentile abs error = 2.27°C. Relative humidity (derived from interpolated T and T_d): daily median bias = +3.09 percentage points; median MAE = 6.61%; median RMSE = 8.38%; median 95th-percentile absolute error = 16.6%; 10-day 95th-percentile = 11.0%. Air temperature interpolation: median daily bias = -0.786°C; median MAE = 1.21°C; median RMSE = 1.47°C; median 95th-percentile abs error = 2.75°C. |
| validation_design | Cross-validation via leave‑one‑station-out comparisons across weather stations in Madagascar: errors summarized as medians across 26 weather stations (Madagascar). For Africa-wide station reporting counts they report numbers: of 1403 GSOD stations, 923 met quality criteria for air temperature (1981–2011), 914 for dew point. Validation compares kriging-predicted distributions to observed station values and to Kriging-predicted error estimates. |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | Authors attribute skill to: (a) removal of systematic seasonal cycle via Fourier decomposition so kriging operates on anomalies with zero mean, (b) use of a high-resolution climate normal (WorldClim) to represent systematic geography/altitude effects and reduce spatial extrapolation error, (c) day-of-year-specific variogram fits capture seasonal changes in spatial correlation length/variability, and (d) altitude correction via observed dew-point lapse rate accounts for orographic effects and moisture decrease with altitude. The method outperforms naïve climatology in areas with station coverage because kriging captures day-to-day weather anomalies; errors are dominated by climate-layer bias far from stations. |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | The paper argues for smoothing variogram/lapse-rate parameters over a 31‑day window (median then mean) to stabilize day-of-year fits given noisy/irregular station reporting; this broad (31-day) pooling reduces variance in parameter estimates while retaining seasonal structure. They imply wide windows help when station samples are limited and when seasonal signals vary smoothly across DOY. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | Quality-control and physical constraints applied: station inclusion criteria (≥61 valid measurements within any 365-day window; no more than 30 consecutive days of zero reporting in DOY histogram; longest missing window ≤30 days), outlier removal for land-surface time series (values >4σ removed and iteratively recomputed), replacement/clip rules for rainfall (RFE 2.0 values >300 mm/day set to 300 mm/day; missing → 0), treatment of pathological MODIS pixels (require ≥61 valid measurements/year or completion from neighbors), optional capping of RH at 100% recommended when interpolated T_d > T_air. Nugget effect considered in variogram when neighboring stations report incongruent values to avoid numerical instability. |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | Reported failure modes: (1) interpolated dew point sometimes exceeds interpolated air temperature producing RH>100%; authors suggest user may cap RH at 100% or interpret as indication of precipitation; (2) Kriging numerical instability/overshoot when semi-variogram lacks nugget or neighboring stations disagree; (3) remote-sensing LST completion fails in very cloudy regions (e.g., southern India monsoon) where large contiguous 'pathological pixels' prevent Fourier extraction; (4) systematic bias due to WorldClim climate-layer error (~<1°C) producing negative bias in predicted T and consequent RH bias. |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | Physical meteorology reasons discussed: (a) orographic precipitation and relief affect dew-point lapse rates and local moisture (environmental dew-point lapse rate larger than air temperature lapse rate, except during dry season), (b) cloudiness affects satellite LST (daytime cooling and nighttime warming) and thus errors in LST-derived temperature fields, (c) regional seasonality (wet vs dry season) changes lapse rates and RH-altitude relationships. Data/model artifacts discussed: (a) sparse/stationary-biased networks and large station-free regions increase kriging error and produce interpolation artifacts, (b) absence of nugget in variogram or unconstrained kriging can overshoot measurements, (c) climate-normal layer bias (WorldClim) introduces systematic offsets, (d) MODIS missing data and aggregation biases (8/16/30-day composites bias clear-sky), (e) RFE satellite limitations (underestimate warm-cloud/orographic precipitation) and clipped rainfall values. Sensor wetting or ventilation issues are noted indirectly as possible short-range measurement errors but not detailed. |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | Authors report: (a) near-equatorial regions have lower 10-day air-temperature variability (~0.5°C) leading to smaller kriging error even when stations are sparse; (b) 10-day temperature variability increases with latitude to ~2.5°C at 30° latitude; (c) dew-point lapse rate is season-dependent in Madagascar and generally larger than air-temp lapse rate except during dry season; (d) relative humidity tends to decrease with altitude except in parts of the dry season; (e) MODIS LST day vs night behaviour differs by land-cover and altitude (daytime LST correlates with land-cover; nighttime LST correlates with altitude). No explicit Koppen-based stratified performance numbers are given, but contrasts between humid lowlands, montane regions, and dry-season behaviour are discussed qualitatively. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | Main equations: (1) Dew point → RH via August–Roche–Magnus: RH = exp( - a b (T - T_d) / ((b + T_d)(b + T)) ) with a=17.271, b=237.7°C. (2) Semi-variogram functional form used for kriging: γ(d) = γ(∞) (1 - 1/(1 - (d/λ)^2)), where γ(∞) is the sill and λ the half-correlation distance, fit per day-of-year. (3) LST reconstruction: LST_ij(t) = MEAN_ij(DOY) + STD_ij(DOY) × [G_ij(t) + E_ij(t) × A_avg(t)], where G is temporal-kriging guess, E remaining error term, and A_avg regional average anomaly. Seasonal decomposition: subtraction of 0-,1-,2-,3-yearly Fourier components (orthogonalized). |
| data_sources | Station data: GSOD (Global Summary of the Day) station air temperature and dew point; WorldClim monthly high-resolution climate normals (used for daily climate layer). Remote sensing: MODIS MYD11A1 v005 LST (Aqua); rainfall: RFE 2.0 (satellite merged estimator), comparisons with GPCC, CRU 2.1. Spatial resolution targeted: ~30 arc-seconds (~1 km) for final products; station records spanning 1981–2010 used for variogram fitting in Madagascar; RFE available from 2001 onward. |
| notable_limitations_caveats | Limitations noted: systematic bias from supporting WorldClim climate layer (~<1°C) affecting absolute temperature/dry-bias; kriging accuracy degrades far from stations and depends on spatial correlation lengths; MODIS LST completion fails in persistently cloudy regions (e.g., Indian monsoon); RFE 2.0 may underestimate warm-cloud/orographic precipitation and 10 years may be insufficient to average rainfall inhomogeneity; interpolation reduces extreme temporal/spatial rainfall variability compared with station-based products; relative humidity interpolation errors dominated by variability and climate-layer errors; authors caution that aggregated remote-sensing composites (8/16/30-day) bias clear-sky conditions and may misrepresent true daily variability. |

metadata.title: Satellite-based near-real-time global daily terrestrial evapotranspiration estimates
metadata.abstract: Abstract. Accurate and timely global evapotranspiration (ET) data are crucial for agriculture, water resource management, and drought forecasting. Although numerous satellite-based ET products are available, few offer near-real-time data. For instance, products like NASA's ECOsystem Spaceborne Thermal Radiometer Experiment mounted on the International Space Station (ECOSTRESS) and MOD16 face challenges such as uneven coverage and delays exceeding 1 week in data availability. In this study, we refined the Variation of the Standard Evapotranspiration Algorithm (VISEA) by fully integrating satellite-based data, e.g., European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ERA5-Land shortwave radiation (which includes satellite remote sensing data within its assimilation system) and MODIS land surface data (which include surface reflectance, temperature and/or emissivity, land cover, vegetation indices, and albedo as inputs). This enables VISEA to provide near-real-time global daily ET estimates with a maximum delay of 1 week at a resolution of 0.05°. Its accuracy was assessed globally using observation data from 149 flux towers across 12 land cover types and comparing them with five other satellite-based ET products and Global Precipitation Climatology Centre (GPCC) data. The results indicate that VISEA provides accurate ET estimates that are comparable to existing products, achieving a mean correlation coefficient (R) of about 0.6 and an RMSE of 1.4 mm d−1. Furthermore, we demonstrated VISEA's utility in drought monitoring during a drought event in the Yangtze River basin in 2022 in which ET changes correlated with precipitation. The near-real-time capability of VISEA is, thus, especially valuable in meteorological and hydrological applications for coordinating drought relief efforts. The VISEA ET dataset is available at https://doi.org/10.11888/Terre.tpdc.300782 (Huang, 2023a).

content.title: VISEA daily near-surface air temperature estimation using the vegetation-index–land-surface-temperature (VI–Ts) triangle method

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | VISEA_Ta_from_VI-Ts |
| name_full | VISEA daily near-surface air temperature estimation using the vegetation-index–land-surface-temperature (VI–Ts) triangle method |
| brief_description | Within the VISEA ET algorithm the authors estimate instantaneous daytime air temperature from the VI–Ts relationship (Nishida et al., 2003) using a local 5×5 grid scatter of VI vs. land surface temperature (Ts), assume the cold-edge Ts equals air temperature for fully vegetated pixels, extend day/night estimates with a sine–cosine diurnal curve, and take the 24 h mean as daily Ta used in subsequent radiation and ET calculations. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | Global application; global 0.05° grid. Validation uses 149 FLUXNET towers (selected from 212) covering 12 IGBP land-cover types (CRO, CSH, DBF, DNF, EBF, ENF, GRA, MF, OSH, SAV, WET, WSA) across tropical humid lowlands, savannas, temperate/needleleaf forests, high-latitude cold regions and other climates. Flux-tower evaluation period mainly 2001–2015 (tower selection) and multi-product comparisons across 2001–2020. |
| target_variable | Daily near-surface air temperature (Ta, K) estimated as a 24 h average derived from satellite instantaneous estimates and sine–cosine diurnal extension; (the paper does not directly reconstruct dew point or vapor pressure). |
| predictors_used | MODIS land surface temperature (MOD11C1 Ts daytime and nighttime), MODIS vegetation index (MOD13C1 VI), neighboring 5×5 grid cell VI–Ts scatter, ERA5-Land hourly downward shortwave radiation (ERA5_Rd) used later for energy budget and daily net radiation, satellite albedo (MCD43C3) and emissivity (from MOD11C1), cloud-clearness index derived from ERA5_Rd, and (for nighttime) MOD11C1 nighttime Ts assumed equal to Ta. No use of simple Tmin-only regressions is reported for Ta estimation. |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | No explicit comparison to FAO-56 assumption Tdew ≈ Tmin or to dew-point-from-Tmin climatologies; VISEA compares radiation sources (ERA5 vs. CERES) and compares final ET against other ET products (GLEAM, FLUXCOM, MOD16, AVHRR, PML) and FLUXNET observations, but not against FAO-56 dew-point baseline. |
| method_model_type | Empirical physical hybrid: VI–Ts triangle method to infer instantaneous air temperature (local per-pixel using neighboring 5×5 grid scatter), interpolation along warm/cold edges to map VI->Ts_min (assumed Ta), then a sine–cosine diurnal fitting to produce hourly Ta profiles and a 24 h mean. This is embedded inside the VISEA Penman–Monteith-based ET framework which uses decoupling-parameter adjustments to convert instantaneous EF to daily EF. No machine-learning, AR, or kriging methods used for Ta estimation. |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | Seasonality handled implicitly via (a) using current-day MODIS VI/Ts observations within a 5×5 spatial neighborhood to create the VI–Ts scatter (no explicit day-of-year pooling reported) and (b) using daily ERA5_Rd and daily cloud-clearness Kt. There is no reported explicit per-day-of-year regression, moving window (e.g., 7/30/45 d) for Ta estimation; gap-filling of missing MODIS days uses neighboring days (no explicit window width reported besides 'neighboring days'); FAO extraterrestrial radiation uses day-of-year (standard FAO formula) for Ra. |
| localization_stratification | Localization via spatial neighborhood (5×5 MODIS grid window) to build the VI–Ts triangle and identify warm/cold edges; flux-tower validation is stratified by IGBP land-cover types. No explicit climate-zone-specific regression models or elevation bands for Ta estimation are fitted within VISEA Ta method. |
| anomaly_definition | No use of anomalies (departures from climatology) or detrending described for Ta estimation; climatologies are used elsewhere (e.g., MODIS multi-year products) but not for anomaly-based Ta reconstruction. |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | None reported. No AR(p) or time-lagged dewpoint/humidity terms used for Ta or humidity reconstruction. |
| accuracy_metrics | Reported skill for VISEA_Ta against FLUXNET observations by land-cover: NSE ranged ~ -0.22 (worst, MF) to 0.82 (best, OSH); correlation R ranged ~0.44 to 0.97; RMSE ranged ~5.7 K (best) to 11.2 K (worst) depending on land-cover. For other variables relevant to humidity inference (ERA5_Rd): mean NSE 0.84, mean R 0.92, RMSE 38.3 W m^-2. ET (dependent product) has mean correlation around 0.6 and RMSE about 1.4 mm d^-1 (abstract); per-land-cover ET NSE values and RMSEs are reported in the paper and Table 3 and Figures 4–7. |
| validation_design | Validation vs. in situ FLUXNET2015 tower data: selected 149 towers fulfilling coverage (2001–2015 period), ERA5_Rd>0, and MODIS land-cover consistency; evaluation compares estimated Ta, net radiation, and ET against tower measurements. Multi-product comparison uses 5 independent gridded ET datasets (GLEAM, FLUXCOM, AVHRR, MOD16, PML) and GPCC precipitation. Validation metrics are computed monthly and daily and stratified by IGBP land-cover type; cross-validation or temporal holdout of training is not applicable because the VI–Ts method is an observational/local empirical procedure rather than a trained statistical model. |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | Authors explain why VI–Ts works: negative correlation between VI and Ts across mixed vegetation/bare patterns (warm edge from bare/dry pixels, cold edge from dense-vegetation pixels) allows estimation of minimum Ts (assumed Ta) via triangle geometry in VI–Ts space. The decoupling parameter (Ω) accounts for radiative vs aerodynamic control, converting instantaneous EF to daily EF, improving daily ET estimates. ERA5 radiation assimilation gives near-real-time energy forcing but errors in ERA5_Rd and mismatch between tower footprint and grid-average albedo/vegetation explain much of the bias. Soil moisture is recognised as a critical regulator for ET (buffering/recovery after rainfall) but is not included in Ta estimation. |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | Authors implicitly prefer local spatial pooling (5×5) rather than broad seasonal pooling because the VI–Ts triangle relies on within-neighborhood contrasts in VI and Ts to identify warm/cold edges; they use neighboring days for gap-filling to reduce cloud-induced noise. No explicit statement that very broad day-of-year smoothing is superior; rather they point out that insufficient VI variance across a neighborhood (e.g., dense forest or homogeneous bare regions) undermines the method, implying a trade-off between sampling variance and locality. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | Assumptions and QC noted: (1) for fully vegetated grid cells the minimum surface temperature is assumed equal to air temperature (Ta); (2) soil heat flux G ≈ 0 on daily basis; (3) excluded flux towers with zero ERA5_Rd and ensured tower site grid cells are land via MOD12C1; (4) emissivity from MOD11C1 used and atmospheric emissivity computed following Brutsaert (1975) and Wang & Dickinson (2013); (5) gap-filling of MODIS data uses neighboring days; (6) no explicit Tdew <= Ta clipping or RH bounds are discussed because dew point/humidity are not estimated directly in the paper. |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | The paper does not report explicit attempts to reconstruct dew point or humidity and thus does not report observed physically implausible dew points; however it reports failure modes of the Ta and ET estimation that would affect any downstream humidity/dew-point estimates: (a) VI–Ts method failure in dense forests, cold-season/temperate regions (positive VI–Ts correlation), and savannas during dry or wet seasons where VI variance is low, and (b) ERA5_Rd poor performance in savannas leading to large errors in net radiation and ET. The authors note systematic underestimation of net radiation (~30%) in some land covers which would bias any vapor-pressure-related reconstructions. |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | Physical meteorology explanations given: (a) VI–Ts failure where vegetation growth correlates positively with Ts (temperate/cold regions) or where vegetation is homogeneous (deserts, dense forests) so warm/cold edges are not present; (b) savanna complexity (seasonal vegetation cover, cloudiness, aerosols, land-use change) complicates radiative transfer and ERA5 radiation simulation; (c) soil moisture buffering causes delayed ET response after rainfall (affects ET but would also affect humidity estimates if used); (d) scale mismatch between flux-tower footprint and 0.05° grid affects Rn comparisons. Data/QC/model artifacts: (a) ERA5_Rd biases (assimilation/model errors) especially over savannas; (b) gap-filling of MODIS (neighboring days) can introduce artifacts when cloud cover is persistent; (c) representativeness errors due to grid-mean albedo differing from tower footprint albedo; (d) the VI–Ts method's assumption that minimum Ts equals Ta may fail and propagate systematic bias into subsequent calculations. |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | Performance varies by land-cover/climate: best Ta performance in open shrubland (OSH), woody savanna (WSA), and grassland (GRA) (high NSE/R and low RMSE), poor performance in mixed forests (MF), savanna (SAV), and some croplands (CRO) where VI–Ts correlation breaks down. ERA5_Rd performs well overall but poorly in SAV (NSE=0.29, RMSE ~63.2 W m^-2). VISEA ET tends to underestimate ET in colder high-latitude regions and shows biases in savannas due to ERA5_Rd and Ta errors. Tropical humid lowlands have very high ET magnitudes (~1500 mm yr^-1) and VISEA can overestimate ET if water availability is not properly constrained. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | Key formulations used (paper equation references): (a) VI–Ts triangle to identify warm/cold edges and map VI to Ts (Nishida et al., 2003, described in paper sect. 2.1.3); (b) EF^i and EF^d relations: instantaneous EF^i (Eq. 4) and conversion to daily EF^d via decoupling parameter Ω and Δ (Eqs. 7–10); (c) daily available energy Q = R_n - G (Eq. 11) with R_n computed from downward shortwave, albedo, emissivities and downward longwave parametrized with cloud clearness (Eqs. 12–16); (d) daily ET^d = EF^d * Q^d (Eq. 17). The explicit Tmin->Tdew formula is not present because dew point is not estimated. |
| data_sources | MODIS products: MOD11C1 (LST/emissivity), MOD09CMG (surface reflectance), MCD43C3 (albedo), MOD13C1 (vegetation index), MCD12C1 (land cover) at 0.05°; ERA5-Land hourly downward shortwave radiation (ERA5_Rd) (0.1°, interpolated to 0.05° for use); FLUXNET2015 towers (149 selected) for validation; additional gridded ET products for comparison: GLEAM, FLUXCOM, AVHRR ET, MOD16, PML; precipitation from GPCC and CPC used in drought case analysis. Time periods: tower comparisons use 2001–2015 (tower selection), multi-product comparisons across ~2001–2020 (varies by product). CERES was used in a sensitivity test for incident radiation. |
| notable_limitations_caveats | Authors note key limitations: (1) VI–Ts fails where VI–Ts negative correlation is absent (dense forests, cold-season/temperate regions, homogeneous bare surfaces), (2) ERA5_Rd biases (especially over savannas) strongly affect net radiation and ET, (3) scale/footprint mismatch between tower (~100–200 m) and 0.05° grids (~25 km^2) introduces errors, (4) MODIS data gaps (~one-third of days) require gap-filling which may reduce accuracy on cloudy days, (5) lack of soil moisture or explicit water-availability state in the algorithm can lead to overestimation of ET in energy-rich but water-limited tropical regions, (6) the method does not estimate dew-point/humidity directly and thus cannot be used immediately for Tmin->Tdew reconstructions without additional conversions and constraints. |

metadata.title: Exploring Design Choices for Autoregressive Deep Learning Climate Models

tldr.text: This study quantitatively compares the long-term stability of three prominent DL-MWP architectures - FourCastNet, SFNO, and ClimaX - trained on ERA5 reanalysis data at 5.625{\deg} resolution, identifying configurations that enable stable 10-year rollouts while preserving the statistical properties of the reference dataset.

metadata.abstract: Deep Learning models have achieved state-of-the-art performance in medium-range weather prediction but often fail to maintain physically consistent rollouts beyond 14 days. In contrast, a few atmospheric models demonstrate stability over decades, though the key design choices enabling this remain unclear. This study quantitatively compares the long-term stability of three prominent DL-MWP architectures - FourCastNet, SFNO, and ClimaX - trained on ERA5 reanalysis data at 5.625{\deg} resolution. We systematically assess the impact of autoregressive training steps, model capacity, and choice of prognostic variables, identifying configurations that enable stable 10-year rollouts while preserving the statistical properties of the reference dataset. Notably, rollouts with SFNO exhibit the greatest robustness to hyperparameter choices, yet all models can experience instability depending on the random seed and the set of prognostic variables

content.title: Multi-step autoregressive training objective

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | multi-step autoregressive training |
| name_full | Multi-step autoregressive training objective |
| brief_description | Training objective that sums prediction losses across M successive autoregressive forecast steps (M ∈ {1,2,4}) with Δt=6 h to mitigate error growth in iterative rollouts. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | Global, coarse (5.625°) ERA5-based WeatherBench1 grid; no sub-regional/climate-zone-specific fitting described. |
| target_variable | All prognostic variables including near-surface temperature (tas) and specific humidity (hus) at multiple pressure levels (used jointly in multi-variable autoregressive forecasts); not targeted specifically to dew-point but relevant to humidity prediction. |
| predictors_used | Full set of prognostic variables (either 8-variable or 33-variable sets including tas and hus), constant fields (lsm, orog, lat, lon) and forcing (tisr). Not a Tmin-only method. |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | Compared against climatology baseline (temporal average over 1979–2007 training period) as lower-bound; no mention or comparison to FAO-56 Tdew≈Tmin or simple Tmin-to-Tdew rules. |
| method_model_type | Deep-learning autoregressive sequence model (ClimaX / FourCastNet / SFNO) trained with multi-step MSE loss summed across M autoregressive steps; not a statistical regression like LOESS/GAM. |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | No per-day-of-year or seasonal local regression described; seasonality handled implicitly by training data spanning 1979–2007 and by using TISR as forcing; no explicit day-of-year windows or harmonic terms. |
| localization_stratification | No geographic or climate-zone stratified fitting; models trained globally on gridded data at 5.625° resolution. |
| anomaly_definition | No anomaly-based training described for predictors or targets (models are trained on z-score normalized absolute variables using global mean and std computed over training set). |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | Explicit autoregressive setup: models forecast next state and are rolled forward; training experiments varied M ∈ {1,2,4} autoregressive steps (Δt = 6 h). Multi-step training (M>1) reduces 10-year rollout RMSE and improves stability. |
| accuracy_metrics | Area-weighted normalized RMSE averaged across evaluated variables (tas, uas, vas, ta850, zg500) and compared to climatology RMSE; values reported qualitatively (RMSE 'close to climatology'); no numerical RMSE table in text (figures show distributions). |
| validation_design | Training: 1979–2007; validation: 2008; testing/rollout initialization: 2009–01-01 00:00 UTC; 10-year autoregressive rollouts (2009–2018). 42368 training samples (sampling 4 initial times per day). Grid-search across architectures, capacities and M; 10 random seeds per configuration. |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | Multi-step training mitigates autoregressive error growth and enhances long-term stability; geometry-aware SFNO implicitly enforces geometrical constraints allowing higher capacity without overfitting. |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | Not applicable for seasonal/day-of-year pooling (no explicit broad smoothing used); implied preference for multi-step objective to reduce accumulation of short-term errors rather than temporal smoothing. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | No explicit physical post-processing constraints (e.g., ensuring Tdew ≤ Tair or RH bounds) applied; variables normalized by global mean/std; relative humidity was omitted from one prognostic set (33-variable set minus RH). |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | No explicit reports of extremely high dew-point values, but some autoregressive rollouts 'completely degenerate' or 'explode' producing physically implausible distributions for some seeds/configurations (instability observed across variables including near-surface quantities). |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | Attributed to model design and training factors: insufficient multi-step training (M=1), inappropriate model capacity (overfitting for ClimaX/FCN when too large), sensitivity to random seed, and choice of prognostic variables; SFNO more robust due to geometry-awareness. Also noted lack of explicit forcing (ocean state/greenhouse gas) can limit realism over decades. |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | No explicit per-climate-zone breakdown; however, authors note instability tied to 'noisy signals close to the poles' when model capacity increases, suggesting polar-region overfitting issues. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | Training loss: L_t = Σ_{m=0}^{M-1} Σ_{k=1}^{Kp} Σ_{h=1}^{H} a_h Σ_{w=1}^{W} (X_{t+mΔt} + f_θ(X_{t+mΔt}, F_{t+mΔt}, C) - X_{t+(m+1)Δt})^2. No Tmin→Tdew parameterization provided. |
| data_sources | WeatherBench1 dataset (hourly ERA5 reanalysis interpolated bilinearly to a regular 5.625° lat-lon grid, covering 1979–2018); prognostic sets include tas and hus among others. Forcing TISR computed from CMIP6 solar forcing (Matthes et al. 2017). |
| notable_limitations_caveats | Coarse spatial resolution (5.625°) may limit applicability to station-scale Tmin→Tdew approaches; models are not forced by ocean/greenhouse gas trends so cannot be expected to beat climatology; sensitivity to random seeds and prognostic variable set; no explicit physical constraints or station-level QC described. |

| target_variable | Same prognostic variables as models (e.g., tas, uas, vas, ta850, zg500); climatology used as benchmark for all evaluated variables including specific humidity (hus) when present. |
| predictors_used | None — climatology is the temporal mean per grid cell computed over the training period. |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | Climatology itself is the baseline; authors explicitly state they use climatology as lower-bound and do not expect models (unforced by ocean/GHG) to outperform it. No FAO-56 or Tmin-based baselines are used or compared. |
| method_model_type | Empirical temporal averaging (grid-cell mean over training years). |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | Climatology computed as temporal average over entire multi-year training period (1979–2007); no explicit day-of-year smoothing/windowing described for the baseline. |
| localization_stratification | Per-grid-cell climatology (spatially local), derived from global gridded dataset. |
| anomaly_definition | Climatology is the baseline; no anomalies used for model inputs in baseline comparisons. |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | Not applicable for climatology baseline. |
| accuracy_metrics | Baseline RMSE computed and used to contextualize model RMSE; models that reach RMSE 'close to climatology' considered successful. Exact numeric RMSEs not tabulated in text. |
| validation_design | Climatology derived from 1979–2007 training period and compared against 10-year test period (2009–2018) rollouts. |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | Climatology acts as a stable long-term estimator since models lack realistic external forcings; used as pragmatic lower bound for 10-year unforced rollouts. |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | Implicit: multi-year averaging reduces internal variability and sets a conservative benchmark; authors emphasize climatology indicates how climate changed between training and evaluation periods. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | Not applicable beyond the underlying ERA5 QC used to produce WeatherBench1. |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | Not applicable for climatology baseline. |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | Not applicable beyond caution that climatology cannot capture forced trends. |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | Climatology is computed globally per grid cell; no specific zone analysis presented. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | Temporal mean (climatology) over training years; no further parameterization. |
| data_sources | Computed from WeatherBench1 (ERA5-based) training years 1979–2007. |
| notable_limitations_caveats | Climatology does not capture externally forced changes (e.g., GHG, ocean state) and may incorporate interpolation artifacts from WeatherBench creation. |

| brief_description | Specific humidity (hus) at multiple pressure levels (925, 850, 700, 600, 500, 250 hPa) is included in the 33-variable prognostic set and used by models to predict humidity-related fields. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | Global ERA5-derived WeatherBench1 grid at 5.625° resolution. |
| target_variable | Specific humidity (hus) itself is predicted in models when included; dew point not explicitly targeted but hus is physically related to vapor pressure and dew point. |
| predictors_used | hus along with tas, winds, geopotential heights, and other atmospheric levels; not a single-Tmin predictor approach. |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | No simple physical conversion baselines (e.g., Tmin→Tdew) compared; models' hus forecasts compared indirectly via RMSE vs climatology. |
| method_model_type | Learned multivariate deep-learning autoregressive models (ClimaX/FCN/SFNO) predicting hus jointly with other prognostic variables. |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | No explicit seasonal/day-of-year stratification for hus modeling; seasonality learned from full training record. |
| localization_stratification | Global gridded training; no station/local hus-specific regressions. |
| anomaly_definition | No explicit anomalies used; variables z-score normalized globally across training period. |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | hus is predicted inside autoregressive rollouts; training experimented with 1–4-step autoregressive objectives to reduce drift in hus forecasts. |

| reported_skill_mechanisms | Including humidity prognostics can both help and harm stability depending on model architecture and capacity; larger prognostic sets destabilized some FCN/SFNO configurations while ClimaX benefited from more variables. |

| brief_description | WeatherBench1 is derived from ERA5 reanalysis and bilinearly interpolated to a 5.625° regular lat-lon grid; this preprocessing and coarse resolution are noted as potential limitations/artifacts. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | Global gridded domain at 5.625°; therefore station-scale microclimates (e.g., Andes valleys, coastal deserts) are not resolved. |
| target_variable | All prognostic variables in WeatherBench1 (tas, hus, winds, geopotential, etc.). |
| predictors_used | Underlying ERA5 variables; authors list prognostic, constant and forcing fields used as model inputs. |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | No Tmin→Tdew baselines used; authors note climatology baseline derived from same interpolated data. |
| method_model_type | Dataset preprocessing: bilinear interpolation from ERA5 to regular grid (WeatherBench1) used as model input; not a modeling method per se but relevant to data artifacts. |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | Dataset contains full diurnal/seasonal cycles across 1979–2018; no additional day-of-year pooling applied in preprocessing. |
| localization_stratification | Dataset includes land-sea mask and orography as constant fields; no station-level data provided. |
| anomaly_definition | Not applicable to interpolation step; models apply z-score normalization using global training means and stds. |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | Temporal resolution kept at 6-hourly Δt (models trained for 6 h steps); rollouts performed at this temporal resolution. |
| accuracy_metrics | Not directly applicable; dataset provenance influences downstream RMSE results. |
| validation_design | WeatherBench split used: 1979–2007 train, 2008 validation, 2009–2018 test; training samples count = 42368 (4 initial times per day). |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | Authors caution that bilinear interpolation and coarse resolution may limit representativeness and that results may not generalize to higher spatial resolutions. |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | Bilinear interpolation and coarse grid smooth fine-scale variability, effectively applying a spatial smoothing that may reduce noise but also remove local extremes relevant to station-level dew point. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | Underlying ERA5 QC properties apply; no additional station-level QC described. Authors removed relative humidity from one prognostic set. |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | No dew-point-specific failures attributed to interpolation, but authors flag potential interpolation artifacts as a caveat for generalization and physical realism. |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | Interpolation/coarse-graining can mask local moisture gradients and cold-air pooling effects; may bias humidity fields relative to station Tmin→Tdew relationships. |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | Coarse grid cannot resolve e.g., Andes elevation contrasts or coastal desert microclimates; authors explicitly note unclear generalization to higher spatial resolutions. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | Bilinear interpolation method used in creating WeatherBench1 from ERA5 (Rasp et al., 2020) as documented by WeatherBench; no further equations provided here. |
| data_sources | WeatherBench1 (Rasp et al., 2020) created from ERA5 (Hersbach et al., 2020) covering 1979–2018 at hourly resolution before interpolation. |
| notable_limitations_caveats | Interpolation artifacts, coarse resolution (5.625°), and absence of station-level QC limit direct applicability to Tmin→Tdew station-scale reconstructions; authors caution on generalization to higher resolution. |

content.title: Autoregressive rollout instability and degenerate/exploding solutions

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | model instability / failure modes |
| name_full | Autoregressive rollout instability and degenerate/exploding solutions |
| brief_description | Observed failure mode where some trained models (dependent on random seed, capacity, and prognostic set) produce degenerate or exploding 10-year rollouts, producing physically implausible distributions for predicted variables. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | Global ERA5-derived grid; instability sometimes traced to noisy signals near the poles but not localized to humid tropical lowlands in the paper. |
| target_variable | All prognostic variables (tas, hus, winds, geopotential); failures manifest in multiple variables simultaneously. |
| predictors_used | Failures occur across model configurations using different prognostic sets (8- and 33-variable sets) and architectures (ClimaX, FCN, SFNO). |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | Failing rollouts produce RMSE much larger than climatology baseline; climatology used to contextualize severity. |
| method_model_type | Observed across deep-learning autoregressive architectures (ClimaX, FourCastNet, SFNO) under certain hyperparameters and seeds. |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | Not implicated as a remedy in the paper; failures occur despite full seasonal coverage in training data. |
| localization_stratification | No spatial stratified retraining described to address failure; failures sometimes associated with polar-region noise when capacity increases. |
| anomaly_definition | No anomaly-based mitigation described; failures occur when models trained on absolute (z-score normalized) fields. |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | Failure risk reduced by multi-step training (higher M) — single-step (M=1) more prone to instability; autoregressive rollout itself is the process where errors compound leading to degeneracy. |
| accuracy_metrics | Instability characterized qualitatively and via large increases in area-weighted normalized RMSE; figures show distributions and some seeds with infinite/very large RMSE (excluded from mean). |
| validation_design | Instability observed during 10-year autoregressive rollouts initialized from 2009–01-01; multiple random seeds (10) per configuration revealed seed-dependent failures. |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | Authors attribute improved robustness primarily to multi-step training and to SFNO geometry-awareness; inadequate capacity choice or too-large capacity (leading to overfitting) is implicated in failures for FCN and ClimaX. |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | Not discussed; paper emphasizes architectural and training-protocol remedies (multi-step objective, appropriate capacity) rather than temporal smoothing. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | No post hoc physical constraint enforcement described to prevent exploding variables (e.g., clipping, conservation enforcement). |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | Paper does not document explicit high dew-point (<-> extremely humid) events or >30–35°C dew points; failures are multivariate degeneracies that could, in principle, produce unphysical humidity/dew-point-like extremes but are not specifically analyzed for dew point. |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | Mechanisms proposed: accumulation of autoregressive errors mitigated by multi-step training; overfitting to noisy polar signals with high-capacity non-geometry-aware models; randomness in initialization (seed sensitivity); missing external forcings (ocean state, GHG) for long-term realism. |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | Authors note noisy signals near poles and mention that some models overfit 'noisy signals close to the poles' when capacity is increased, but do not provide tropical/dry-season failure diagnostics. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | No special equation beyond training loss; failure diagnosis qualitative and based on RMSE and visual inspection of rollouts (timeseries and maps in appendix). |
| data_sources | Failures observed on WeatherBench1 (ERA5-derived) 5.625° dataset for 10-year rollouts (2009–2018) across multiple model configurations and random seeds. |
| notable_limitations_caveats | Authors stress that demonstrations at coarse resolution may not generalize to higher resolutions; lack of physical constraint enforcement and unforced setup (no ocean coupling) are key caveats for interpreting stability and failure modes. |
