metadata.title: Improving Subseasonal Forecasting in the Western U.S. with Machine Learning

tldr.text: This work presents and evaluates the machine learning approach to the Rodeo and releases the SubseasonalRodeo dataset, collected to train and evaluate the system, an ensemble of two nonlinear regression models.

journal.name: Proceedings of the 25th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery & Data Mining

metadata.abstract: Water managers in the western United States (U.S.) rely on longterm forecasts of temperature and precipitation to prepare for droughts and other wet weather extremes. To improve the accuracy of these longterm forecasts, the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) launched the Subseasonal Climate Forecast Rodeo, a year-long real-time forecasting challenge in which participants aimed to skillfully predict temperature and precipitation in the western U.S. two to four weeks and four to six weeks in advance. Here we present and evaluate our machine learning approach to the Rodeo and release our SubseasonalRodeo dataset, collected to train and evaluate our forecasting system. Our system is an ensemble of two nonlinear regression models. The first integrates the diverse collection of meteorological measurements and dynamic model forecasts in the SubseasonalRodeo dataset and prunes irrelevant predictors using a customized multitask feature selection procedure. The second uses only historical measurements of the target variable (temperature or precipitation) and introduces multitask nearest neighbor features into a weighted local linear regression. Each model alone is significantly more accurate than the debiased operational U.S. Climate Forecasting System (CFSv2), and our ensemble skill exceeds that of the top Rodeo competitor for each target variable and forecast horizon. Moreover, over 2011-2018, an ensemble of our regression models and debiased CFSv2 improves debiased CFSv2 skill by 40-50% for temperature and 129-169% for precipitation. We hope that both our dataset and our methods will help to advance the state of the art in subseasonal forecasting.

content.title: Local Linear Regression with Multitask Feature Selection (MultiLLR)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | MultiLLR |
| name_full | Local Linear Regression with Multitask Feature Selection (MultiLLR) |
| brief_description | A locally-weighted linear regression that selects predictors jointly across all grid points via a customized multitask backward stepwise procedure tuned to the cosine-similarity skill objective; locality is defined by day-of-year windows and coefficients are fit per grid point. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | Western contiguous United States (25°N–50°N, 125°W–93°W) at 1°×1° grid; Köppen–Geiger climate classifications are included in the dataset and elevation is provided; study emphasizes mid-latitude western U.S. context (includes coastal, inland, mountainous regions). |
| target_variable | Primary targets: tmp2m (average of daily tmax and tmin, °C) and total precipitation (mm) aggregated over two-week periods; relative humidity (rhum) and other moisture variables are included as predictors. The paper does NOT reconstruct daily dew point (Tdew) or vapor pressure directly. |
| predictors_used | Candidate regressors included: tmin, tmax, tmp2m, tmp2m anomalies and statistics (std), surface pressure (pres), surface relative humidity (rhum, sigma=0.995), precipitable water (pr_wtr), precipitation (precip), potential evaporation (pevpr), SST and sea-ice PCs, MEI, MJO phase/amplitude, geopotential height PCs (10mb etc.), NMME model means/forecasts, elevation, Köppen–Geiger class; many features appear with lagged versions and anomaly transforms (suffix 'anom' used). |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | Compared against climatology (month-day climatology over 1981–2010 used to form anomalies) and a debiased CFSv2 operational forecast baseline (reconstructed); damped persistence baseline was an official Rodeo baseline (no exact reconstruction). FAO-56 heuristic Tdew ≈ Tmin is NOT mentioned or compared. |
| method_model_type | Weighted local linear regression with multitask (joint across grid points) backward stepwise feature selection optimized for cosine-similarity skill; regressions fit per-grid-point after feature selection. Offsets (climatology) and datapoint weighting used. Feature selection removes predictors iteratively using LOYOCV skill. Complexity noted: O(nd^2 + Y d^3) per grid point per step. |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | Locality determined by day-of-year using a centered window; training data restricted to a 56-day span (s = 56 days) around the target day-of-year for most tasks (explicitly stated). For precipitation MultiLLR used 56-day span; MultiLLR's locality/window choice is used to select seasonally-local models. |
| localization_stratification | Localization via day-of-year window (56-day) pooled across all years; feature selection is multitask across all grid points but coefficients differ per grid point. Climate-zone data (Köppen–Geiger) and elevation are available as spatial covariates but MultiLLR localization is primarily temporal (day-of-year). |
| anomaly_definition | Anomalies defined as a_t = y_t - c_monthday(t), where c_d is the climatology for month-day combination d computed as the 30-sample average over 1981–2010 (c_d = (1/30) sum_{t: monthday(t)=d, 1981<=year(t)<=2010} y_t ). Many features include 'anom' versions (feature values are anomalies relative to their climatologies). |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | MultiLLR candidate feature set includes lagged measurements (shiftl indicators) drawn from available lags; exact lags depend on data source and update frequency. The AutoKNN model (separate) uses explicit lags of 29/58/365 days for weeks 3–4 and 43/86/365 days for weeks 5–6 (see AutoKNN entry). |
| accuracy_metrics | Skill metric used is spatial cosine similarity between forecast anomaly vector and observed anomaly vector (cosine of anomaly vectors). Reported mean contest-period skills (examples): temperature weeks 3–4: MultiLLR 0.3079, AutoKNN 0.2807, ensemble 0.3451, debiased CFSv2 0.1589 (Table 1). Historical (2011–2017) multi-year mean skills: temp weeks 3–4 MultiLLR 0.2344, AutoKNN 0.3111; precip weeks 3–4 MultiLLR 0.1567, AutoKNN 0.1513 (Table 2). No RMSE/MAE for dew point (not estimated). |
| validation_design | Feature selection and model evaluation employ leave-one-year-out cross-validation (LOYOCV) on the target day-of-year; for LOYOCV the authors hold out one year's worth of data around the target date (with specific holdout ranges: weeks 3–4 hold out 29 days before t through 335 days after t; weeks 5–6 hold out 43 days before through 321 days after t). Contest-period evaluation: 26 biweekly forecast dates (Apr 18, 2017–Apr 17, 2018). Historical evaluation: yearly sequences Apr 18 of year to Apr 17 next year for 2011–2017 using only data prior to each forecast issue date. |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | Authors attribute improved skill to combining diverse predictors, tailoring models to day-of-year locality, multitask feature selection (which picks locally relevant features), and capturing analog nearest-neighbor patterns; no discussion specific to Tmin→Tdew relationships. They note that NMME's lower utility for temperature may be due to temporal (monthly) granularity mismatch with biweekly targets. |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | The 56-day day-of-year pooling is used to strike a balance between locality (seasonal dependence) and sample size; broader pooling was not explicitly justified beyond locality suitability and LOYOCV-driven selection. The paper implies that seasonally-local models reduce errors relative to global/long-window approaches because they capture the day-of-year–dependent predictor relevance. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | Modeling enforces climatology offsets (b_{t,g} = c_monthday(t,g)) so regressions target anomalies; weighted regressions use 1/variance of target anomaly vector in AutoKNN. No explicit physical constraints (e.g., Tdew ≤ Tair, RH bounds clipping) are reported. Data QC: interpolation uses distance-weighted interpolation with requirements (e.g., NCL opt@critpc = 50% present to interpolate) and missing data replaced by averages in some CFS procedures. |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | None |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | Not applicable for Tdew since dew point reconstruction is not performed; paper does identify potential data/model issues such as mismatch of NMME monthly granularity with biweekly target periods leading to degraded NMME contribution, and the official baselines exhibiting extreme negative skill values (causing lower means). Authors do not discuss sensor wetting, reanalysis humidity biases, or boundary-layer coupling as causes in this work. |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | Dataset includes Köppen–Geiger climate regions and elevation; MultiLLR selects different predictors with different frequencies by task (Fig.2): pres, ones (intercept), and tmp2m are top features across tasks; NMME ensemble mean is selected more often for precipitation than temperature. No explicit per-Köppen performance breakdown reported for moisture or dew-point estimation because dew point was not estimated. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | Climatology/anomaly: a_t = y_t - c_{monthday(t)} with c_d = (1/30) Σ_{t: monthday(t)=d, 1981≤year(t)≤2010} y_t. Forecast skill: skill(â_t, a_t) = cos(â_t, a_t) = ⟨â_t, a_t⟩ / (\|\|â_t\|\|_2 \|\|a_t\|\|_2). Local regression solved via least squares per gridpoint: β̂_g = argmin_β Σ_{t∈D} w_{t,g} (y_{t,g} - b_{t,g} - β^T x_{t,g})^2. Ensemble: average of ℓ2-normalized anomaly forecasts: â_ensemble = 0.5 * (â_multillr/\|\|â_multillr\|\|_2) + 0.5 * (â_autoknn/\|\|â_autoknn\|\|_2). |
| data_sources | CPC Global Gridded Temperature (tmax, tmin, tmp2m) 1979–, CPC Gauge-Based Precipitation (global and CONUS) 1948/1979–, NOAA OISST (SST & sea-ice) 1981–, NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis (rhum, pres, pr_wtr, geopotential heights) 1948–, MEI 1949–, MJO (BOM) 1974–, NMME models and forecasts (various models), elevation dataset, Köppen–Geiger classification. Data interpolated to 1°×1° grid and aggregated to 14-day target windows. |
| notable_limitations_caveats | Paper does NOT estimate daily dew point or vapor pressure; moisture variables are used as predictors but dew-point reconstruction methods and failure modes (e.g., unrealistic high dew points in tropics or sensor wetting) are not discussed. Other caveats: NMME monthly granularity mismatch with biweekly targets reduces usefulness; damped persistence exact form not available for reproduction; contest CFSv2 baseline uses 4 initializations but only one initialization was available in archive so reconstructed baseline is approximate. |

content.title: Multitask k-Nearest Neighbor Autoregression (AutoKNN)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | AutoKNN |
| name_full | Multitask k-Nearest Neighbor Autoregression (AutoKNN) |
| brief_description | A weighted local linear regression using only historical measurements of the target variable; features include fixed lagged anomalies (recent and 1-year lag) and anomaly patterns from the top-k most similar past dates identified by a cosine-skill-based similarity over preceding anomaly sequences. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | Western contiguous United States (25°N–50°N, 125°W–93°W) at 1°×1° grid; applied to the same regional targets as MultiLLR. |
| target_variable | tmp2m (°C average of tmax and tmin) and precipitation (mm) aggregated over two-week periods; AutoKNN does not reconstruct dew point, but uses target-variable anomalies and lagged target anomalies as predictors. |
| predictors_used | Only features derived from the target variable: lagged anomalies at specific lags (29, 58, 365 days for weeks 3–4; 43, 86, 365 days for weeks 5–6), constant intercept, and nearest-neighbor anomaly vectors (knn1...knn20 for temperature; knn1 only for precipitation). Similarity computed using mean skill over H=60 days of preceding anomalies (lag ℓ = 365). |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | Performance compared to debiased CFSv2 and climatology-based anomaly baseline; FAO-56 Tdew≈Tmin not mentioned. |
| method_model_type | Nearest-neighbor–enhanced autoregression: identify top-k historically similar dates using skill-based similarity of preceding anomaly sequences (Algorithm 3), scale neighbor anomaly vectors to unit std, then regress current anomaly on fixed lags + knn features via weighted local linear regression with locality potentially determined by day-of-year (precipitation) or using all dates (temperature). |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | For precipitation prediction, training data restricted to a 56-day day-of-year window; for temperature prediction AutoKNN used all dates (no day-of-year locality). Similar neighbors for precipitation tend to come from the same month/season as target (Fig.3/Fig.4). |
| localization_stratification | Locality: day-of-year window for precipitation, none for temperature. Multitask: neighbor selection and regression performed jointly across grid points for similarity but final regressions are per-grid-point with weighting (w_{t,g} = 1/var(target anomaly vector)). |
| anomaly_definition | Uses the same anomaly definition: a_t = y_t - c_{monthday(t)} where climatology c is computed from 1981–2010 monthly/day-of-year means; neighbors and lags use anomaly series. |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | Explicit lags: for weeks 3–4 predictions include anomalies at 29 days, 58 days, and 365 days prior; for weeks 5–6 use 43 days, 86 days, and 365 days. These lags chosen based on data availability windows (most recent obs available 29 days prior for weeks3–4 etc.). Nearest-neighbor features are computed using similarity over H=60-day preceding windows lagged by one year (ℓ = 365). |
| accuracy_metrics | Same cosine-similarity skill metric reported. AutoKNN contest-period skills (Table 1): temperature weeks 3–4 0.2807, weeks 5–6 0.2817; precipitation weeks 3–4 0.2156, weeks 5–6 0.1870. Historical mean skills (2011–2017) in Table 2: temp weeks3–4 mean 0.3111, precip weeks3–4 mean 0.1513. |
| validation_design | Nearest-neighbor selection and model fitting respect real-time availability (only dates observed prior to issuance considered viable). LOYOCV used for feature selection in MultiLLR; AutoKNN neighbor selection performed per-target-date using historical anomalies and then regressions trained excluding unavailable future data. Historical evaluation across years 2011–2017 with only pre-forecast data used for training. |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | Authors argue that using similar historical anomaly patterns (skill-based analogs) captures recurring spatial anomaly structures and improves skill, especially for precipitation where seasonal analogs are strong. For temperature, neighbors are drawn from diverse months, consistent with recent warming trends changing analog selection. |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | For precipitation, seasonally-restricted training and neighbor selection imply that seasonal pooling helps because precipitation anomaly patterns are strongly seasonal; for temperature, broader pooling (all dates) was used due to different neighbor-month patterns. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | No physical constraints on moisture variables or dew point applied; regressions operate on anomaly vectors with weighting; neighbor anomalies scaled to unit standard deviation prior to inclusion. |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | None |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | Not applicable for dew-point estimation; AutoKNN failure modes for precipitation/temperature not discussed in terms of physical boundary-layer processes or sensor issues. Authors do note that analogs for temperature in recent years tend to be drawn from recent years (post-2010), reflecting nonstationarity. |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | For precipitation, top neighbors generally match the season of the target date (Fig.3/4) indicating strong seasonal behavior; for temperature, neighbors come from across the year and recent years are over-represented, indicating nonstationarity or trend effects. No explicit per-Köppen performance metrics for humidity/dew point. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | Similarity: sim_t = (1/H) Σ_{h=0}^{H-1} skill(a_{t-ℓ-h}, a_{t'-ℓ-h}) with H=60 and ℓ=365; knn features are the anomaly vectors of most similar dates scaled to unit sd. Regression as weighted least squares onto {lagged anomalies, ⃗knn features, ones}. |
| data_sources | Uses the SubseasonalRodeo dataset target-variable time series derived from CPC tmp2m and precipitation (interpolated and aggregated to 14-day windows). |
| notable_limitations_caveats | AutoKNN relies solely on the target variable history and nearest-neighbor analogs; it does not incorporate explicit moisture predictors like rhum or pr_wtr. The analog approach may be sensitive to nonstationarity (recent warming), which is observed as neighbors for temperature coming disproportionately from recent years. |

content.title: Leave-One-Year-Out Cross-Validation Backward Stepwise Multitask Feature Selection

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | LOYOCV Backward Stepwise |
| name_full | Leave-One-Year-Out Cross-Validation Backward Stepwise Multitask Feature Selection |
| brief_description | A customized backward stepwise feature selection procedure that uses leave-one-year-out cross-validated (LOYOCV) cosine-similarity skill averaged over years for the target day-of-year to remove predictors that least reduce LOYOCV skill until a tolerance threshold is reached. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | Applied for western U.S. 1°×1° grid forecasts; the selection is performed for each target date's day-of-year pooling across years. |
| target_variable | Used for tmp2m and precipitation anomaly forecasting (not for dew point). |
| predictors_used | Operates on candidate predictor set including lagged measurements (temperature, humidity, pressure, NMME, SST PCs, MEI, MJO, etc.) and their anomaly transforms. |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | Feature selection objective is LOYOCV skill relative to climatology-based anomalies; no explicit FAO-56 comparison. |
| method_model_type | Backward stepwise removal: at each step compute LOYOCV skill with each candidate removed; drop the candidate whose removal yields the largest LOYOCV skill (i.e., least harm) if improvement exceeds tol (tol=0.01). Multitask selection: variables selected jointly for all grid points, coefficients still fit per grid point. |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | Selection is performed per target day-of-year using training dates with that day-of-year across years and locality windows (the LOYOCV folds hold out date ranges surrounding the target date to avoid leakage). |
| localization_stratification | Feature selection is multitask across all grid points (joint selection), but regressions (fits) are per-grid-point after selection. |
| anomaly_definition | Uses same anomaly definition (departures from month-day climatology computed 1981–2010). |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | Lagged candidate predictors are included in the candidate set and can be removed or retained by the selection procedure; specific lags for AutoKNN are enumerated elsewhere. |
| accuracy_metrics | Selection objective is average LOYOCV cosine-similarity skill across years for the given day-of-year; threshold tol = 0.01 applied to stop selection. |
| validation_design | LOYOCV folds: for weeks 3–4 hold out 29 days before t through 335 days after t; for weeks 5–6 hold out 43 days before through 321 days after t. Average skill across held-out years used to guide selection. |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | Selection tailored to maximize the cosine-similarity skill objective directly, enabling retention of only those predictors that improve spatial anomaly alignment across years for that day-of-year. |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | Procedure implicitly balances seasonally-local modeling (selection per day-of-year) with sample size across years; the 56-day window and LOYOCV ensure models are tuned for local seasonal structure without using near-future dates. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | No explicit physical constraints imposed within selection; selection purely skill-driven. Data interpolation QC described elsewhere. |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | None |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | Not discussed for dew point; general caveats include potential overfitting if the LOYOCV objective poorly represents out-of-sample variability, and reduced efficacy if predictors have mismatched temporal resolution (e.g., monthly NMME vs biweekly targets). |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | Not reported; selection performed globally over western-U.S. grid points with joint selection across grid points. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | Algorithm 2 described: selection compares LOYOCV skill ν and ν_j (skill with j removed) and removes j* maximizing ν_j if tol > ν - max_j ν_j, else converge. |
| data_sources | Operates on SubseasonalRodeo dataset features drawn from CPC, NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis, OISST, MEI, MJO, NMME, etc. |
| notable_limitations_caveats | Complexity O(nd^2 + Y d^3) per grid point per step; average d 20–23, average number of steps 13 in experiments — computationally intensive but parallelized. Feature selection driven by the cosine-skill objective which may not penalize certain physically implausible predictor relationships if they improve spatial alignment. |

content.title: Reconstructed Debiased Operational CFSv2 Forecast

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Debiased CFSv2 (reconstructed) |
| name_full | Reconstructed Debiased Operational CFSv2 Forecast |
| brief_description | An approximation of the contest baseline debiased CFSv2 forecast reconstructed by averaging selected operational CFSv2 forecasts and applying a debiasing correction computed from 1999–2010 CFS reforecast averages and observed 1999–2010 month-day climatology. |
| citation_title |  |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | Used as a benchmark for the western contiguous U.S. contest grid; reconstructed from available operational CFSv2 archives for 2011–2018 evaluation. |
| target_variable | Provided forecasts for 2‑meter temperature (tmp2m) and precipitation (2-week sums/rates) aggregated to contest target windows; used as baseline anomalies relative to climatology. Not used to estimate dew point. |
| predictors_used | Physics-based dynamical model (CFSv2) forecasts; reconstruction averages available initializations/leadtimes (approximation used because only one initialization archive accessible). |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | Compared directly to ML methods and climatology-based anomalies; the reconstructed debiased CFSv2 baseline is intended to approximate the official Rodeo debiased-CFSv2 baseline. No FAO-56 comparison. |
| method_model_type | Operational dynamical model (CFSv2) outputs debiased by subtracting long-term mean CFS reforecast (1999–2010) and adding observed 1999–2010 month-day mean to form a debiased forecast for the target monthday. |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | Debiasing uses month-day (monthday) climatology over 1999–2010 for corrections; reforecast averages computed per monthday. |
| localization_stratification | Forecasts are gridded output from CFSv2 and then interpolated to contest 1°×1° grid; debiasing applied per grid cell/monthday. |
| anomaly_definition | Debiasing uses observed 1999–2010 monthly/day climatology and long-term CFS reforecast averages over 1999–2010; contest anomaly definition uses 1981–2010 climatology for scoring, but reconstructed debiasing used 1999–2010 reforecast period per contest guidance. |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | Not applicable; CFSv2 is a dynamical forecast model producing direct predictions at lead times. |
| accuracy_metrics | Reconstructed debiased CFSv2 contest-period skills (Table 1) example: temperature weeks 3–4 0.1589, weeks 5–6 0.2192; precipitation weeks 3–4 0.0713, weeks 5–6 0.0227. Historical multi-year mean skills (2011–2017) reported in Table 2 per year. |
| validation_design | Reconstructed from archived operational forecasts and reforecasts; compared to ML models on same biweekly forecast dates (real-time emulation) for contest and historical periods. |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | Authors note that ML ensembles (with CFSv2) improve skill substantially; they also note that NMME and coarse temporal resolution can reduce physics-based model contributions for biweekly targets. |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | Debiasing is done using long-term reforecast averages over 1999–2010 (monthly/day-of-year), a broad climatological adjustment to remove systematic model bias. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | CFSv2 includes physical constraints inherent in dynamical modeling; no additional QC in the reconstruction beyond interpolation and missing-data averaging. |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | None |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | Authors cite mismatch of monthly NMME or reforecast granularity with biweekly target periods and limited archived initializations as sources of imperfect baseline reconstruction; do not discuss dew-point-specific measurement artifacts. |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | Reconstructed baseline skill varies year-to-year; no detailed breakdown by climate zone in relation to humidity or dew point. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | Debiasing: reconstructed_CFS = raw_CFS_forecast - mean_CFS_reforecast_{1999-2010, monthday} + observed_mean_{1999-2010, monthday}. |
| data_sources | CFSv2 Operational Forecast dataset (6-hourly) and CFS Reforecast High-Priority Subset (1999–2010) from NCEI/NOAA archives, interpolated to 1° grid; bilinear interpolation and 2-week aggregation applied. |
| notable_limitations_caveats | Reconstruction approximates the official debiased-CFSv2 baseline because only one initialization archive was available; missing forecast initializations and monthly granularity issues can affect the reconstructed baseline's fidelity to the contest baseline. |

content.title: Surface Relative Humidity (rhum at sigma level 0.995) from NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Relative Humidity (rhum) in Dataset |
| name_full | Surface Relative Humidity (rhum at sigma level 0.995) from NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis |
| brief_description | Surface relative humidity near 2 m (sigma 0.995) from NCEP/NCAR reanalysis is included among candidate predictors in the SubseasonalRodeo dataset and used by MultiLLR as a frequently-selected predictor for both temperature and precipitation tasks. |
| citation_title |  |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | Provided on a global grid and interpolated to the western U.S. 1°×1° contest grid; reanalysis spans 1948–present. |
| target_variable | rhum (near-surface relative humidity), used as predictor; dew point Tdew not directly estimated from rhum in this paper. |
| predictors_used | rhum used as a direct predictor (raw and anomaly versions possible) alongside pres, pr_wtr, tmp2m, etc.; pr_wtr (precipitable water) also included from reanalysis. |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | No explicit baseline comparisons for using rhum to derive dew point; rhum used as feature compared indirectly by selection frequency against other predictors. |
| method_model_type | rhum is included as a candidate covariate for MultiLLR local linear regression; selection frequency shown in Fig.2 indicates relative importance across tasks. |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | rhum enters models that are trained on day-of-year local windows (56-day) for MultiLLR; anomalies of rhum may be included ('anom' suffix) consistent with paper-wide anomaly definition. |
| localization_stratification | As a spatially-varying predictor it is interpolated to contest grid; selection is multitask across grid points but coefficients fit per-grid-point. |
| anomaly_definition | rhum anomalies would be defined consistent with other variables as departures from 1981–2010 month-day climatology if 'anom' version used; paper indicates some features use 'anom' suffix. |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | rhum can appear with lagged versions in the candidate set (shiftl suffix), but the paper does not detail specific rhum lag inclusion frequencies; MultiLLR candidate set includes lagged measurements based on data source frequency. |
| accuracy_metrics | No separate accuracy metrics reported for rhum → target relationships; importance inferred from feature-selection frequency plots (Fig.2). |
| validation_design | rhum used in LOYOCV-based feature selection and local regression training similar to other predictors. |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | Paper does not provide a physical mechanism mapping rhum to dew point estimates (not performed) but uses rhum as a predictor likely to add moisture information relevant to precipitation and temperature anomaly forecasts. |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | rhum is treated like other predictors within the day-of-year locality/window framework; no explicit discussion about smoothing for rhum. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | rhum from NCEP/NCAR reanalysis is a reanalysis product; the paper does not discuss reanalysis humidity biases or apply physical clipping/constraints on rhum in models. |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | None |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | Not discussed in context of rhum→Tdew conversion; paper does note general data issues like interpolation and temporal-granularity mismatch for some predictors (e.g., NMME). |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | Selection frequency of rhum as predictor is high across tasks (Fig.2); no per-climate-zone performance metrics given for rhum-based contributions. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | No explicit psychrometric conversion or Tdew formula provided; rhum left as numeric predictor in regression frameworks. |
| data_sources | NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis rhum at sigma level 0.995 (surface-near), daily from 1948–present, interpolated and aggregated to 14-day target windows on 1°×1° grid. |
| notable_limitations_caveats | Authors do not discuss reanalysis humidity biases, sensor wetting, or other QC issues for rhum; reanalysis and interpolation choices (e.g., remapdis) are described in dataset appendix but potential biases of reanalysis humidity for dew-point conversion are not explored. |

content.title: ℓ2-normalized Averaging Ensemble (Proposition 1 ensemble)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Ensemble ℓ2-normalization |
| name_full | ℓ2-normalized Averaging Ensemble (Proposition 1 ensemble) |
| brief_description | An ensemble strategy that ℓ2-normalizes individual model predicted anomaly vectors and averages them, which mathematically guarantees that when the average of individual anomaly skills is positive the ensemble skill is strictly greater than that average. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | Applied to ensemble MultiLLR + AutoKNN and also to a three-component ensemble including reconstructed debiased CFSv2 for western U.S. grid forecasts. |
| target_variable | Applied to anomaly forecasts of tmp2m and precipitation aggregated over two-week windows; not used to combine dew-point reconstructions because none performed. |
| predictors_used | Ensembles combine whole-model anomaly forecasts (each model may have different predictors); ensemble itself takes normalized anomaly vectors as inputs. |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | Compared ensemble skill to average individual skills and to debiased CFSv2 baseline and top Rodeo competitor performance. |
| method_model_type | Averaging of ℓ2-normalized anomaly vectors: â_ensemble = Σ p_i (â_i / \|\|â_i\|\|_2) with equal weights in experiments (p_i=1/2 for two-model ensemble). Proposition 1 proves ensemble skill improvement when mean individual skill positive. |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | Ensembling performed per-target-date after individual model predictions which may be seasonally localized; ensemble does not itself re-pool across season. |
| localization_stratification | Ensemble is global across grid points (applied to full anomaly vectors) but each member produces localized per-grid-point forecasts. |
| anomaly_definition | Ensures all members' outputs are anomaly forecasts (each model uses climatology offset b_{t,g}=c_monthday(t,g) such that regressions predict anomalies). |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | Ensemble itself has no AR terms; member models (AutoKNN) include lag terms. |
| accuracy_metrics | Ensemble improved skills relative to individual models; contest-period ensemble skill examples (Table 1): temp weeks 3–4 ensemble 0.3451 vs MultiLLR 0.3079 and AutoKNN 0.2807; precipitation weeks 3–4 ensemble 0.2364 vs MultiLLR 0.1597 and AutoKNN 0.2156. Three-member ensemble (MultiLLR+AutoKNN+rec-deb-CFSv2) further improved skill (Table 2). |
| validation_design | Ensembles evaluated on contest-period real-time dates and historical yearly sequences; ℓ2-normalization and ensembling performed per target date prior to computing skill. |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | Mathematical guarantee (Proposition 1) demonstrates ensemble ℓ2-normalized averaging yields skill at least as large as (and strictly larger than, when average positive) the average of member skills because of vector normalization and cosine-angle properties. |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | Ensembling mitigates extreme negative skill events (histograms in Fig.1) and stabilizes forecasts across dates; normalization prevents domination by large-magnitude member forecasts. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | No physical constraints introduced by ensembling; ensemble acts on anomaly vectors without clipping to physical ranges. |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | None |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | Not applicable to dew point; ensemble reduces extreme negative skills seen in some baselines but does not address physical implausibility of variables not modeled. |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | No explicit per-climate-zone ensemble diagnostics for dew point or humidity; ensemble gains consistent across the four forecasting tasks in the western U.S. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | Proposition 1: normalized ensemble vector ā_{(p)} = Σ p_i (â_i / \|\|â_i\|\|_2) and equality sign relations linking mean individual cosines to ensemble cosine; ensemble improves skill whenever average member skill positive (see proposition in text). |
| data_sources | Applies to model outputs from MultiLLR and AutoKNN (trained on SubseasonalRodeo dataset) and reconstructed debiased CFSv2 outputs. |
| notable_limitations_caveats | Ensemble improves cosine-similarity skill but does not impose variable-wise physical constraints (e.g., RH bounds, dew point ≤ temperature). |

metadata.title: An open-source MEteoroLOgical observation time series DISaggregation Tool (MELODIST v0.1.1)
metadata.abstract: Abstract. Meteorological time series with 1 h time steps are required in many applications in geoscientific modelling. These hourly time series generally cover shorter periods of time compared to daily meteorological time series. We present an open-source MEteoroLOgical observation time series DISaggregation Tool (MELODIST). This software package is written in Python and comprises simple methods to temporally downscale (disaggregate) daily meteorological time series to hourly data. MELODIST is capable of disaggregating the most commonly used meteorological variables for geoscientific modelling including temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind speed, and shortwave radiation. In this way, disaggregation is performed independently for each variable considering a single site without spatial dependencies. The algorithms are validated against observed meteorological time series for five sites in different climates. Results indicate a good reconstruction of diurnal features at those sites. This makes the methodology interesting to users of models operating at hourly time steps, who want to apply their models for longer periods of time not covered by hourly observations.

content.title: Humidity disaggregation method H1: daily dew-point equal to daily minimum temperature (T_dew = T_min)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | H1 (Tdew = Tmin) |
| name_full | Humidity disaggregation method H1: daily dew-point equal to daily minimum temperature (T_dew = T_min) |
| brief_description | A deterministic baseline used in MELODIST that assumes daily dew-point temperature equals the daily minimum air temperature (no diurnal dew-point variation). Cited implementations: Bregaglio et al. (2010); Waichler & Wigmosta (2003). |
| citation_title | An open-source MEteoroLOgical observation time series DISaggregation Tool (MELODIST v0.1.1) |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | Multi-site study across climates: De Bilt (Netherlands, mid-latitude, low elevation ~2 m), Ny-Ålesund (Svalbard, polar, ~11 m), Obergurgl (Alpine, high elevation 1938 m), Rio de Janeiro – São Cristovão (humid tropical lowland, ~5 m), Tucson International Airport (arid/subtropical desert, ~779 m). The paper evaluates methods on these five stations spanning polar, alpine, temperate and arid/tropical climates. |
| target_variable | Dew-point temperature (T_dew) and derived relative humidity (H, %). (Equations in paper use °C for Magnus formula and dew-point calculation; some internal units represented in K in parts of the text.) |
| predictors_used | Daily minimum temperature (T_min) only for H1 (no additional covariates required). In practice hourly air temperature (disaggregated T) is required to compute hourly RH from daily T_dew. |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | H1 itself is the simple baseline (T_dew = T_min) frequently referenced in literature (e.g., Bregaglio et al., Waichler & Wigmosta). The paper treats H1 as a no-calibration deterministic baseline against which more complex methods (H2,H3,H4) are compared qualitatively. |
| method_model_type | Deterministic identity rule (T_dew_day = T_min_day). Implemented per-station (single-site), no fitting required. |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | None — H1 does not pool by season or day-of-year; it uses daily minima directly. |
| localization_stratification | Single-station application; no spatial pooling or climate-zone stratification (the whole MELODIST framework is station-local). |
| anomaly_definition | None (no anomalies used). |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | None. |
| accuracy_metrics | The paper does not present a dedicated table for H1 performance, but discusses that H1 (T_dew = T_min) is a common simple choice and that calibrated methods generally outperform naive approaches; specific quantitative metrics are provided for H3 (see other entries). |
| validation_design | Split-sample validation per station (calibration and independent validation periods listed in Table 1). The same station-by-station split-sample strategy would be applied if H1 were compared in the split-sample test (paper uses split-sample for methods requiring calibration). |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | Paper notes H1 is simple and can be adequate in some settings because dew and humidity typically peak near sunrise; however it omits diurnal variation and may be inadequate when radiation/cloudiness/advection decouple Tmin from ambient moisture. The paper references prior literature (Bregaglio et al., Waichler & Wigmosta) for use of this baseline. |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | Not applicable to H1; the paper discusses broader pooling and smoothing strategies for calibrated methods and cautions overfitting with small samples. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | No explicit clipping beyond physical calculation when converting to RH via Magnus formula; H1 produces a single daily T_dew which is then used with hourly T to compute RH via the Magnus formula (so the calculation enforces the physical relationship e_a = e_s(T_dew)). |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | The paper does not report observations of unrealistically high dew-point values caused by H1 specifically. The authors caution generally that simple methods may be inadequate in special circumstances (e.g., polar night at Ny-Ålesund). |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | Paper notes factors that can decouple Tmin from ambient moisture and hence invalidate H1 in practice: cloudiness and reduced radiative cooling, polar-night conditions, local microclimates (mountain-valley winds), advection and synoptic forcing (general statement that fronts can shift Tmin/Tmax timing). It also highlights data issues (instrument changes, non-homogeneity) as general sources of poor parameter estimation. |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | Paper does not present H1-specific per-climate quantitative comparisons, but overall humidity disaggregation results show best performance in Rio de Janeiro (humid tropical lowland) for the H3 method and notably poor performance at Ny-Ålesund (polar) for calibrated methods, implying simple assumptions like H1 may behave variably by climate. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | Identity: T_dew_day = T_min_day. RH then computed hourly by H = 100 * e_s(T_dew)/e_s(T_air) with e_s given by Magnus formula (Eq. 4 in paper). |
| data_sources | Station data described in Table 1: KNMI De Bilt, AWI Ny-Ålesund (Maturilli et al.), Obergurgl project data, Alerta Rio São Cristovão, NOAA/NREL Tucson; multi-decadal and multi-year records, split into calibration and validation periods (see Table 1 for exact ranges). |
| notable_limitations_caveats | H1 ignores diurnal T_dew variability and can be unrealistic when Tmin is not representative of nocturnal moisture (e.g., during cloud-covered nights, polar night, or when Tmin is influenced by advection). The paper emphasizes the general limitation of simple, non-calibrated methods. |

content.title: Humidity disaggregation method H2: daily dew-point estimated from a linear regression T_dew_day = a*T_min + b

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | H2 (linear regression) |
| name_full | Humidity disaggregation method H2: daily dew-point estimated from a linear regression T_dew_day = a*T_min + b |
| brief_description | A deterministic, site-calibrated linear regression estimating daily dew-point from daily minimum temperature (parameters a, b fitted using available hourly T and H observations). Hourly RH is then computed by converting the T_dew to vapour pressure via Magnus formula. |
| citation_title | An open-source MEteoroLOgical observation time series DISaggregation Tool (MELODIST v0.1.1) |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | Applied and evaluated in the same multi-site framework as above (De Bilt, Ny-Ålesund, Obergurgl, Rio de Janeiro, Tucson). Calibration requires local hourly records; the study uses split-sample station-wise calibration/validation. |
| target_variable | Daily dew-point temperature (T_dew_day) used to compute hourly relative humidity (H, %). |
| predictors_used | Daily minimum temperature (T_min) as the predictor for the regression T_dew_day = a*T_min + b; calibration uses observed hourly temperature and humidity to derive a and b. |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | Compared conceptually to H1 (a=1,b=0) and to H3/H4 approaches in the study; H2 is an intermediate (simple calibrated) model. |
| method_model_type | Simple linear regression (site-specific) between T_min (daily) and daily T_dew; deterministic once calibrated. Calibration uses historical hourly T and H to derive T_dew via Magnus inversion and then regress daily T_dew on T_min. |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | The paper describes calibration as site-specific but does not prescribe seasonal stratification for H2; calibration is done on the station's calibration period (split-sample) and thus implicitly pools across that period unless user applies monthly/seasonal fits. |
| localization_stratification | Per-station calibration (single-site). No across-station pooling or spatial regression was applied in the paper. |
| anomaly_definition | None described for H2; regression is applied on raw daily Tmin vs T_dew_day pairs derived from calibration data. |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | None (H2 is an instantaneous regression on daily Tmin). |
| accuracy_metrics | The paper does not present H2-specific aggregated metrics in a table; H2 is described as a calibrated alternative to H1. Quantitative results in the paper focus on H3 (with full diurnal reconstruction) and H4 (if min/max humidity available). |
| validation_design | Split-sample test per station: calibration of a, b on calibration period (Table 1) and validation on independent validation period (Table 1); number of stations = 5 with multi-year records (exact years per station in Table 1). |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | Calibration allows H2 to adjust for site-specific Tmin–Tdew offsets (e.g., due to typical nocturnal cooling vs moisture availability). The paper notes that calibration improves performance over the naive H1 where site climatology departs from T_dew≈T_min. |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | Paper cautions about parameter estimation reliability when calibration sample sizes are small or non-homogeneous; recommends split-sample testing to avoid overfitting. No explicit kernel/window widths for seasonal pooling provided for H2. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | T_dew_day is obtained consistent with the Magnus relation via inversion of ea from observed T and H during calibration. No additional clipping beyond the physical conversion is documented. |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | No explicit cases of H2 producing extreme/unphysical dew points are reported in the paper. The authors emphasize calibration dependence and potential failure when calibration data are non-homogeneous or limited. |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | Potential failure drivers described include non-homogeneous station records (instrument changes), limited hourly data for robust calibration, and climatic regimes (e.g., polar night) where Tmin is a poor predictor of dew-point; also cloudiness and advection can weaken the Tmin–Tdew coupling. |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | Paper does not present H2-specific per-climate metrics; it reports that calibrated approaches generally perform better than uncalibrated ones and that Rio de Janeiro yielded better humidity reconstruction overall (for H3), indicating that calibration may particularly help in some climates. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | T_dew_day = a * T_min + b (a,b obtained by least-squares fit using derived T_dew from hourly observations via Magnus inversion). Magnus formula (Eq. 4) and inversion (Eq. 6) are used for computing empirical T_dew for calibration. |
| data_sources | Same station data described in Table 1; calibration requires historical hourly T and H observations from the station calibration period. |
| notable_limitations_caveats | Reliant on station-specific calibration data quality and length; nonstationarity in climate or instrumentation may degrade transferability; paper recommends split-sample testing and warns about limited hourly observation availability for robust parameter estimation. |

content.title: Humidity disaggregation method H3: daily T_dew varies linearly between days with an added sinusoidal diurnal variation

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | H3 (diurnal linear + sine) |
| name_full | Humidity disaggregation method H3: daily T_dew varies linearly between days with an added sinusoidal diurnal variation |
| brief_description | A deterministic method that reconstructs hourly dew-point by (1) setting daily mean dew-point per day, (2) linearly interpolating T_dew between consecutive days, and (3) adding a small sinusoidal diurnal correction term (parameters include k_r controlling the sine period). Recommended kr = 6 for months with mean radiation > 100 W m^-2, otherwise kr = 12 (Debele et al., 2007). |
| citation_title | An open-source MEteoroLOgical observation time series DISaggregation Tool (MELODIST v0.1.1) |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | Applied and evaluated at the five study sites spanning polar (Ny-Ålesund), alpine (Obergurgl), temperate (De Bilt), tropical lowland (Rio de Janeiro), and arid (Tucson) environments; calibration/validation via split-sample per station. |
| target_variable | Hourly dew-point temperature (T_dew_hour) used to compute hourly relative humidity (H, %). |
| predictors_used | Daily dew-point per day (T_dew_day) which itself is obtained from a T_dew_day = a*T_min + b style relation (H1/H2) or provided as daily dew-point; uses T_dew_day on day d and d+1 and a sinusoidal correction term (function of hour h) to produce hourly T_dew. The method depends indirectly on Tmin (for daily T_dew_day), and requires disaggregated hourly air temperature (T_hour) to compute RH. |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | Compared against simpler H1/H2 policies and H4 when daily min/max RH available. H3 is the primary evaluated model for humidity disaggregation in the paper (Table 4 reports quantitative validation metrics for H3). |
| method_model_type | Deterministic diurnal interpolation model: (Eq. 7) T_dew(d,h) = T_dew_day(d) + (h/24)*(T_dew_day(d+1) - T_dew_day(d)) + T_dew,Δ(h) where T_dew,Δ(h) is a sinusoidal correction defined in Eq. 8. kr (period parameter) set based on monthly mean radiation. T_dew_day is either taken as T_min (H1) or fitted (H2). Implemented per-station. |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | Seasonality enters via kr selection which depends on average monthly radiation (>100 W m^-2 -> kr=6 else kr=12); otherwise linear interpolation uses consecutive days (implicitly local day-to-day smoothing). No explicit moving-window bandwidths (e.g., 7d/30d) are given for this humidity method. |
| localization_stratification | Per-station application; parameters (e.g., kr selection, T_dew_day regression) are station-specific and can be calibrated using local hourly observations. |
| anomaly_definition | Not used; method interpolates raw daily T_dew values between consecutive days. |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | Uses consecutive-day values (T_dew_day(d+1) and T_dew_day(d)), i.e., an explicit day-to-day dependency (one-step persistence/interpolation), but no explicit AR(p) time-series modeling with lag coefficients is used. |
| accuracy_metrics | Table 4 in the paper reports H3 performance (validation period) per station (values are hourly-statistics): - De Bilt: observed mean RH 81.82%, model mean 81.63%; std obs 15.12%, std model 15.48%; RMSE 12.67%; r = 0.66; NSE = 0.30. - Ny-Ålesund: mean obs 74.96%, model 74.82%; std obs 12.61%, std model 12.30%; RMSE 17.41%; r = 0.02; NSE = -0.91 (very poor phase skill). - Obergurgl: mean obs 70.83%, model 66.42%; std obs 17.67%, std model 13.40%; RMSE 16.43%; r = 0.51; NSE = 0.14. - Rio de Janeiro: mean obs 70.95%, model 67.45%; std obs 14.13%, std model 10.76%; RMSE 10.39%; r = 0.72; NSE = 0.46. - Tucson: mean obs 35.31%, model 33.31%; std obs 21.96%, std model 10.51%; RMSE 18.52%; r = 0.55; NSE = 0.29. (These RMSE/r/NSE values are hourly measures over the validation period.) |
| validation_design | Split-sample test per station. Five stations used; calibration and validation periods are station-specific as listed in Table 1 (examples: De Bilt: calibration 1961–1990, validation 1991–2014; Ny-Ålesund: calibration 1993–2004, validation 2006–2011; other stations likewise have ~decadal calibration/validation windows). Evaluations use the independent validation periods and hourly aggregated observations. |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | The paper attributes H3's ability to reconstruct diurnal RH patterns to (a) the typical diurnal behaviour of humidity (maximum near sunrise, minimum in early afternoon) and (b) the fact that mean daily dew point tends to occur around sunrise; the sinusoidal correction captures the small within-day variation. It also notes that H3 performance depends on prior temperature disaggregation quality and on radiation/cloud control of diurnal amplitude. Rio de Janeiro showed the best H3 performance (higher r and NSE), while Ny-Ålesund performed poorly (likely due to polar-night conditions and weak/irregular diurnal forcing). |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | H3 effectively applies a short (1-day) linear smoothing (inter-day linear interpolation) plus a small sinusoidal intraday correction. The authors caution that parameter choices (kr) depend on monthly mean radiation and that limited hourly observation availability can limit confident parameter estimation; they recommend split-sample testing to avoid overfitting. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | Dew-point and RH are calculated using the Magnus formula (Eq. 4) ensuring the thermodynamic relationship between T_dew and vapour pressure is preserved. The method uses physically consistent inversion (Eq. 6). No additional hard clipping thresholds are described for preventing T_dew > T_air; the Magnus-based conversion enforces thermodynamic consistency when applied correctly. |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | No explicit report of the method producing physically implausible high dew points. However, Ny-Ålesund produced very poor correlation (r≈0.02) and negative NSE for H3 — indicating the model can fail where diurnal forcing is weak/atypical (polar night) or when the prior temperature disaggregation is not appropriate. |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | Paper-identified causes for poor H3 performance include: polar-night/low-radiation regimes (Ny-Ålesund) that invalidate diurnal assumptions; errors propagated from temperature disaggregation; changes in station instrumentation or data inhomogeneity; cloudiness reducing diurnal amplitude; local microclimates (mountain/valley winds) that change timing of minima/maxima; and limited hourly data for calibration. |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | H3 performance varied by climate: best performance metrics at Rio de Janeiro (humid tropical lowland; RMSE ≈ 10.4%, r ≈ 0.72, NSE ≈ 0.46), moderate performance at De Bilt and Obergurgl, poor performance at Ny-Ålesund (polar) with negligible correlation and negative NSE, and relatively poor RMSE but moderate correlation at Tucson (arid). The paper highlights that availability of daily min/max RH (H4) improves performance where available. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | Eq. 7: (T_dew)_{d,h} = (T_dew_day)_d + (h/24) * ((T_dew_day)_{d+1} - (T_dew_day)_d) + (T_dew,Δ)_h. Eq. 8: (T_dew,Δ)_h = (1/2) * sin((h+1)*π/k_r - 3π/4). kr recommended = 6 for months with mean monthly radiation > 100 W m^-2, else kr = 12. T_dew_day often obtained by T_dew_day = a*T_min + b (H2/H1). Magnus saturation formula Eq. 4 and inversion Eq. 6 used for conversions. |
| data_sources | Station datasets in Table 1: De Bilt (KNMI), Ny-Ålesund (AWI / Maturilli et al.), Obergurgl (project data), Rio de Janeiro – São Cristovão (Alerta Rio), Tucson (NOAA/NREL). Calibration/validation periods per station listed in Table 1. |
| notable_limitations_caveats | H3 depends on accurate estimation of daily T_dew_day (from Tmin or regression) and on reasonable diurnal forcing (radiation-driven). Performance degrades in regimes with weak/atypical diurnal cycles (polar night) or where Tmin is not representative of nocturnal moisture. Parameter kr selection is heuristic (radiation threshold 100 W m^-2). Authors caution about data homogeneity, instrumentation changes, and limited hourly data for robust parameter estimation. |

content.title: Humidity disaggregation method H4: hourly RH from daily minimum and maximum relative humidity combined with disaggregated hourly temperature

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | H4 (min/max RH interpolation) |
| name_full | Humidity disaggregation method H4: hourly RH from daily minimum and maximum relative humidity combined with disaggregated hourly temperature |
| brief_description | A deterministic redistribution that uses daily H_min and H_max together with disaggregated hourly air temperature (T_hour) and daily Tmin/Tmax to compute hourly RH by linear interpolation across the diurnal temperature cycle (Eq. 9 in the paper). |
| citation_title | An open-source MEteoroLOgical observation time series DISaggregation Tool (MELODIST v0.1.1) |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | Applied in the same multi-site evaluation framework; H4 requires that daily H_min and H_max are available (not all stations provided both). Paper notes H4 is the preferred option when those daily humidity extremes are available. |
| target_variable | Hourly relative humidity (H, %), constructed directly from observed daily H_min/H_max and disaggregated hourly temperature. |
| predictors_used | Daily H_min and H_max (observed), daily Tmin and Tmax and disaggregated hourly temperature T_hour (from the temperature disaggregation method), used together in a linear redistribution formula. |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | H4 is compared conceptually as the best available option when daily H_min/H_max are available; it is described as superior to H1–H3 when both H_min and H_max exist because it explicitly preserves daily humidity extremes. |
| method_model_type | Deterministic linear interpolation (Equation 9): H_hour = H_max + (T_hour - T_min)/(T_max - T_min) * (H_min - H_max). No calibration required beyond having daily min/max values and disaggregated T_hour. |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | None required — H4 operates on each day individually using that day's H_min, H_max, Tmin, Tmax and hourly T. |
| localization_stratification | Single-station application; relies on that station's reported daily H_min/H_max (no cross-station pooling). |
| anomaly_definition | None. |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | None. |
| accuracy_metrics | Paper states that H4 is the best available option among presented methods if daily min/max RH values are available, but does not present a separate metric table exclusively for H4. Overall humidity metrics (Table 4) correspond to H3 which used only daily single-value inputs; H4 qualitatively described as superior when min/max RH exist. |
| validation_design | Split-sample station-based validation; H4 evaluation is referenced by comparison to H3/H2 in discussion (where daily H_min/H_max are available, H4 recommended). |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | H4 explicitly preserves daily humidity extremes so it better matches observed diurnal RH amplitude and timing when daily H_min/H_max are available; authors state that H4 'is the best available option among all available disaggregation methods' if H_min and H_max are recorded daily (Waichler & Wigmosta, 2003). |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | Not applicable — H4 uses single-day extremes directly and does not perform smoothing across days. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | Uses physically consistent hourly T_hour (disaggregated) combined with observed daily H extremes; does not require additional inversion via Magnus formula because it operates directly on RH. Preserves daily min/max humidity values. |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | Paper does not report H4 producing unrealistic dew points; rather H4 is recommended when daily humidity extremes are available because it preserves observed extremes (reducing the chance of unrealistic smoothing). |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | Potential issues arise when H_min/H_max are missing or inaccurate, and errors in the prior temperature disaggregation propagate into H_hour via the linear interpolation formula. Station data inhomogeneity or measurement errors in reported H_min/H_max would degrade results. |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | Authors state H4 should be preferred wherever daily H_min/H_max are available, implying it performs well across climates compared to methods that only use single daily humidity values; no numeric per-climate H4 table provided. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | Eq. 9: H = H_max + ((T - T_min)/(T_max - T_min)) * (H_min - H_max), where T is hourly temperature (disaggregated), and H_min/H_max and T_min/T_max are daily values. |
| data_sources | Requires daily H_min/H_max from station recordings (available at some study sites); the paper's station list (Table 1) indicates which variables were available per site. |
| notable_limitations_caveats | H4 depends on the availability and quality of daily H_min and H_max; if those are not recorded or are inhomogeneous, H4 cannot be used and simpler methods (H1–H3) must be applied, which reduces skill. |

content.title: Magnus saturation vapour pressure formula and inversion for dew-point calculation (Alduchov & Eskridge, 1997 variant)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Magnus formula (e_s, inversion) |
| name_full | Magnus saturation vapour pressure formula and inversion for dew-point calculation (Alduchov & Eskridge, 1997 variant) |
| brief_description | The paper uses the Magnus formula to compute saturation vapour pressure e_s(T) and its inversion to derive dew-point temperature from actual vapour pressure; this is the physical basis for converting between dew-point and relative humidity. |
| citation_title | An open-source MEteoroLOgical observation time series DISaggregation Tool (MELODIST v0.1.1) |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region_context | Used for all stations and methods that convert between T, T_dew and RH across the five study sites spanning polar, alpine, temperate and arid/tropical climates. |
| target_variable | Saturation vapour pressure e_s (hPa); actual vapour pressure e_a (hPa); dew-point temperature T_dew (°C). |
| predictors_used | Air temperature T (°C) and relative humidity H (%) are used to compute e_a = e_s(T) * H/100; inversion of Magnus yields T_dew from e_a. |
| baseline_assumptions_compared | Not a baseline per se — used as the thermodynamic conversion in all humidity-related methods (H1–H4). |
| method_model_type | Deterministic physical formula. Eq. 4 gives e_s(T) using two parameterizations for T≥0°C and T<0°C (Alduchov & Eskridge coefficients). Eq. 6 gives the inversion to yield T_dew from e_a. |
| seasonal_dayofyear_pooling | Not applicable — purely local physics-based conversion. |
| localization_stratification | Global physical formula applied per-station; no localization required. |
| anomaly_definition | Not applicable. |
| autoregressive_or_lag_terms | Not applicable. |
| accuracy_metrics | Not applicable (used as physical conversion). |
| validation_design | Not applicable to formula usage; formula used to compute diagnostics and calibrate regression-based methods. |
| reported_skill_mechanisms | Magnus formula provides physically consistent mapping between temperature and saturation vapour pressure ensuring that T_dew and RH are thermodynamically consistent with air temperature. |
| interpretation_of_broad_smoothing | Not applicable. |
| physical_constraints_or_qc | By construction, using e_s(T_dew) = e_a enforces consistency between dew-point, vapour pressure, and air temperature; thus implicit constraint that computed e_a cannot exceed e_s(T) without producing T_dew > T (which would indicate supersaturation in the input data). The paper does not describe additional clipping rules beyond the Magnus-based computations. |
| failure_modes_extreme_dewpoint | The paper does not report Magnus formula-induced artifacts; however, if input H or T are erroneous (sensor errors), inversion can yield unrealistic T_dew (this data-quality caveat is noted generally in the paper). |
| hypothesized_failure_mechanisms | Data quality problems (erroneous RH or T inputs due to sensor wetting, ventilation issues, instrument changes) could lead Magnus inversion to produce implausible T_dew values; the paper highlights data homogeneity and instrumentation changes as general concerns. |
| climate_zone_specific_findings | Magnus formula is the physics basis across all climates in the study; differences in performance of downstream disaggregation methods reflect climatic factors rather than the formula itself. |
| key_equations_or_parameterizations | Eq. 4 (Magnus): e_s = 6.1078 * exp(17.08085*T/(234.175 + T)) for T >= 0°C; alternative coefficients for T < 0°C. Eq. 6 gives inversion formula for T_dew from e_a. Eq. 3: H = 100 * e_a/e_s(T). |
| data_sources | Used in converting observed hourly temperature and humidity records from the station datasets (Table 1) into dew-point for calibration and validation. |
| notable_limitations_caveats | Formula is an approximation; paper cites Alduchov & Eskridge (1997) improved Magnus form. More generally, reliable conversion depends on quality of input T and H; the authors emphasize station data homogeneity, instrumentation changes, and QC as important caveats. |
